title: Bundlemorphometry: Spatially Resolved White Matter Bundle Shape Analysis Using Nonlinear Streamline-Based Registration
abstract: ABSTRACT Diffusion MRI tractometry quantifies microstructural properties along white matter (WM) bundles but does not directly measure their geometry, potentially overlooking localized morphological alterations. Here, we introduce BundleMorphometry, a framework for quantifying local WM bundle shape using the analytical Jacobian of nonlinear streamline-based registration. Individual subject bundles are registered to a reference atlas bundle using BundleWarp, a streamline-based nonlinear registration method. We derive the analytical Jacobian of the resulting deformation field and compute its log-determinant (log det J) to quantify local expansion and compression at each streamline point. To enable spatially resolved group comparisons, these measurements are projected onto the two-dimensional grid, capturing variations along and across each bundle. We evaluated BundleMorphometry using two clinical datasets comprising patients with glioma and Parkinson’s disease (PD). In the glioma dataset, BundleMor-phometry revealed spatially extensive deformation patterns in lesion-affected WM bundles that were not captured by displacement magnitude alone. Additionally, in a group analysis of the PD dataset (32 patients and 32 healthy controls), we identified significant localized morphological differences in the corpus callosum forceps major, mid-body and right spinothalamic tract, with distinct patterns of expansion and compression. These findings demonstrate the potential of BundleMorphometry to advance conventional tractometry by enabling spatially resolved analysis of bundle morphology.

title: Generalizable virtual staining from histopathology to spatial proteomics across biological scales
abstract: Large histology archives capture morphological correlates of molecular tissue states but lack direct spatial protein measurements. In this study, we show that routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) histology can provide a queryable, morphology-based representation of spatial protein expression that remains informative from pixels to patients. To achieve this, we developed QUEST, a model framework that represents protein markers as semantic queries for flexible multiplex immunofluorescence (MIF) prediction. Trained on a heterogeneous atlas of paired H&E and MIF images comprising over 10,000 tissue regions, QUEST captured morphological patterns associated with protein markers and reconstructed their expression intensities across diverse tissue types and cohorts. Its utility extended beyond image reconstruction and preserved biologically meaningful information across multiple scales: virtual staining preserved protein marker expression at the cellular and tissue scales, supported cell phenotyping, cellular neighborhood analysis, and characterization of spatial tissue organization, retained clinically relevant signals for patient stratification, and enabled H&E-based queries to retrieve MIF references with similar molecular profiles. These findings position virtual staining not simply as image generation but as a flexible interface between routine histology and spatial proteomics, expanding the analytical value of existing H&E archives.

title: RyR2-Mediated Ca 2+ Leak Drives Progressive Arrhythmogenic Cardiomyopathy
abstract: ABSTRACT Background Abnormal sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) Ca 2+ release through ryanodine receptor 2 (RyR2) is a well-established mechanism of ventricular arrhythmias. Whether persistent RyR2 dysfunction can also initiate the structural remodeling characteristic of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (ACM) remains unknown. We tested the hypothesis that chronic RyR2-mediated Ca 2+ leak is sufficient to couple electrical instability to progressive cardiomyopathy. Methods We generated a rabbit carrying the severe gain-of-function RyR2-V2475F mutation and characterized disease progression using longitudinal cardiac phenotyping, continuous electrocardiographic monitoring, cellular electrophysiology and Ca 2+ imaging, histopathology, biochemical analyses, and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq). Therapeutic potential was evaluated by continuous treatment with the selective RyR2 inhibitor ent -verticilide for two months. Results RyR2-V2475F rabbits developed spontaneous ventricular tachyarrhythmias, sudden cardiac death, and progressive right ventricular (RV)-dominant fibrofatty cardiomyopathy recapitulating major features of human ACM. Malignant ventricular arrhythmias preceded overt structural remodeling and were associated at the cellular level with early spontaneous Ca 2+ release and early afterdepolarizations. Early disease was characterized by remodeling of excitation-contraction coupling with preserved SR Ca 2+ load and contractile function despite RyR2 dysfunction; upon disease progression, these compensatory changes were accompanied by SR Ca 2+ depletion, impaired RV contractility and reduced left ventricular filling. Single-nucleus transcriptomics identified early fibroblast expansion and predicted cardiomyocyte-centered paracrine signaling before advanced fibrofatty infiltration. Cardiomyocytes also exhibited an altered lipid-metabolic transcriptome and intracellular lipid accumulation, accompanied by enhanced mitochondrial Ca 2+ uptake. Selective RyR2 inhibition markedly reduced ventricular tachycardia burden and preserved RV contraction and LV filling during disease progression. Conclusions Severe RyR2 gain-of-function can lead to both malignant ventricular arrhythmias and progressive arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy in a large-animal model, establishing persistent intracellular Ca 2+ dysregulation as a mechanistic link between electrical and structural heart disease. The ability of selective RyR2 inhibition to suppress arrhythmias and preserve cardiac function identifies RyR2 as a potentially actionable therapeutic target in arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy.

title: Peripheral immune biomarkers, brain imaging phenotypes and treatment response in major depressive disorder
abstract: Immune dysregulation is implicated in major depressive disorder (MDD), but its links to clinical features and in vivo brain phenotypes remain uncertain. We examined ten plasma biomarkers in 36 unmedicated MDD patients and 48 control participants using high-sensitivity immune profiling at baseline, alongside PET/MR imaging of brain serotonin transporter (SERT) binding and regional structural measures. Patients underwent three months of antidepressant treatment and were followed up with MR imaging. Glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) was higher in MDD patients (β = 0.66, 95% CI 0.22 - 1.11), and interleukin-33 (IL-33) correlated with subcortical volumes across all participants (β = 0.22, 95% CI 0.07 - 0.38). No marker correlated with SERT binding or cortical thickness after correction, and neither SERT binding nor brain structural measures differed by diagnosis. In the longitudinal analysis, interleukin-13 (IL-13) was associated with greater antidepressant response during first-line treatment with escitalopram (β = 1.09, 95% CI 0.56 - 1.61). IL-15 and IL-13 showed nominal associations with hippocampal volume increase after treatment. These findings support astroglial involvement in MDD and link peripheral immune variation to subcortical brain structure. IL-13 is a candidate prognostic marker of response to selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. Its tentative association with longitudinal changes in hippocampal volume suggests that immune processes in MDD may be related to both the capacity for clinical improvement and brain structural plasticity during treatment.

title: Investigating AI's potential in risk-stratifying lung cancer screenings for extending screening intervals and reducing workload: A retrospective analysis of a tertiary hospital cohort
abstract: ObjectiveWe aimed to 1) evaluate whether AI algorithms could identify a very low-risk sub-population Lung-RADS 1/2 cases suitable for a safe switch to biennial screening, and 2) externally validate Sybil, an imaging-based deep learning lung cancer risk prediction tool. Materials and methodsWe gathered all lung cancer screenings (LCSs) from a tertiary safety-net hospital (n=3120, up to September 2024), manually extracted relevant clinical data, and analyzed Sybils performance across various subgroups, with a specific focus on Lung-RADS 1 and 2 cases. We simulated LCS interval extension using Sybil and the Brock model risk scores calibrated on a subset of the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST). Confidence intervals were obtained through bootstrapping. ResultsThe median follow-up was 2.3 years (interquartile range 1.5-3.1), with a total 6-year cancer incidence rate of 2.3% (72/3120). Lung-RADS 1 and 2 cases comprised 90.5% of our scans. Sybils overall area under the curve (AUC) ranged from 0.819 to 0.912; while its 2-year AUC for Lung-RADS 1 and 2 cases was 0.746. In the screening interval extension simulation, calibrating for a 30% shift to biennial screening translated into 33.8% of negative screens in our data being safely extended using Sybil, with no delayed cancers. The Brock model demonstrated an AUC of 0.513 on our data, with a sensitivity of 18.2% using the 1.5% threshold. ConclusionSybil has the potential to safely extend LCS intervals for low-risk individuals, reducing radiology workload and opening spots for life-saving new screenings. Key pointsO_LIWe investigated whether AI risk stratification tools could identify the lowest-risk individuals undergoing lung cancer screening suitable for switching to a biennial screening schedule. C_LIO_LIIn our simulations, Sybil reduced follow-up screening load by at least 30% through switching the lowest-risk Lung-RADS 1 and 2 cases to biennial screening without delayed cancer diagnoses. C_LIO_LIVery low-risk individuals, as predicted by AI algorithms, could potentially be placed on biennial screening schedules, reducing radiology department workload and freeing time for new patients. title: Olfactory Function in Preclinical Alzheimer’s Disease: A Multi-Cohort Study
abstract: Introduction Olfactory impairment is an early feature of Alzheimer’s disease (AD). However, it is unclear if olfactory performance reflects early pathological changes during preclinical AD and/or predicts subsequent clinical progression among characterized cognitively normal (CN) individuals. We aimed to determine whether odor identification differs by amyloid status, relates to medial temporal lobe (MTL) tau burden and morphometry, and predicts longitudinal conversion to mild cognitive impairment (MCI). title: Rapid Detection and Initial Treatment of Life-Threatening Subdural Hematoma in a Sheep Model
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is the leading cause of death and disability in people under 40 worldwide. There is an unmet need for detection and treatment of life-threatening TBI when computed tomography (CT) scanners and neurosurgeons are unavailable. We developed a new handheld frequency-domain multidetector infrared hemorrhage detection device. Using the new device, military pre-hospital medics required <4 minutes to detect life-threatening subdural hematoma in a sheep model. We developed a second device that allows non-neurosurgeons to safely create a burr hole and partially remove clotted subdural blood. In sheep, the treatment device reduced intracranial pressure within 20 minutes, and improved post-anesthesia blinded neurological outcomes. With human use adaptation, these devices could allow rapid detection and initial treatment of some life-threatening TBIs in challenging situations.

title: Late radiation-induced brain injury is associated with functional cerebrovascular impairment without structural vessel loss in mice
abstract: ABSTRACT Background Radiation-induced brain injury (RIBI) is a major and often irreversible complication of cranial radiotherapy, affecting up to 90% of long-term survivors. Although cerebrovascular damage is a leading mechanistic hypothesis, whether chronic resting hypoperfusion occurs independently of structural vessel loss remains unknown. The aim of this study was to comprehensively characterize cerebrovascular, structural, and behavioral outcomes in a murine model of late RIBI to determine the primary drivers of vascular dysfunction. Methods Adult C57BL/6 mice underwent 12 Gy whole-brain irradiation and were assessed one year later using laser speckle contrast imaging (LSCI), 7T MRI, immunohistochemistry, and behavioral testing. Results Irradiated mice exhibited reduced pial flow velocity and flow area by LSCI, indicative of upstream cerebrovascular dysfunction, while bulk cortical tissue perfusion was preserved. This pial hypoperfusion was accompanied by cerebral atrophy, decreased T2* relaxation time and tissue iron deposition consistent with chronic microhemorrhage across multiple brain regions by MRI, blood-brain barrier disruption reflected by reduced ZO-1 and VE-cadherin expression, and increased anxiety-like behavior. Strikingly, capillary density, pericyte coverage, astrocyte endfeet, and NeuN-positive neuronal nuclei were all preserved. Conclusion These findings demonstrate that functional vascular impairment - not structural vessel or neuronal loss - drives hypoperfusion and blood-brain barrier disruption in late RIBI. This dissociation between vascular dysfunction and rarefaction reframes the pathophysiology of RIBI and identifies endothelial dysfunction as a tractable therapeutic target for intervention.

title: Cortical Thinning in Adults with Prader–Willi Syndrome: Distribution Across Functional Networks and Associations with BMI and the GH/IGF-1 Axis
abstract: Prader–Willi syndrome (PWS) is a rare neurogenetic disorder associated with neuropsychiatric, metabolic, endocrine, and physical abnormalities. Although previous neuroimaging studies have identified regional gray matter alterations, cortical thickness (CT) abnormalities and their distribution across large-scale functional brain networks remain poorly characterized in adults with PWS. We investigated cortical morphology in 23 adults with PWS and 22 age- and sex-matched healthy controls who underwent structural MRI. Cortical reconstruction and surface-based morphometric analyses were performed using FreeSurfer. Between-group differences in CT were assessed using age, sex, and intracranial volume as covariates. Associations between CT and clinical, cognitive, anthropometric, and endocrine measures were examined using Spearman correlations. Significant cortical regions were further mapped onto an a priori functional network atlas. Adults with PWS showed reduced CT in a left-hemispheric cluster involving the inferior precentral gyrus, insula, inferior temporal cortex, and orbitofrontal cortex. This cluster overlapped predominantly with the somatomotor, auditory, cingulo-opercular, language, and frontoparietal networks. Within the PWS group, lower CT was associated with higher body mass index and poorer global functioning. CT was positively associated with IGF-1 levels and was greater in participants with a history of growth hormone therapy during childhood. These findings indicate cortical thinning across regions belonging to multiple functional networks involved in sensorimotor, attentional, language, and executive processes, extending previous volumetric findings. The associations with body mass index, functional measures, and the GH/IGF-1 axis suggest that cortical morphology may reflect an interplay between genetic vulnerability and potentially modifiable metabolic and endocrine factors, raising the possibility of a neuroprotective role for GH/IGF-1 signaling.

title: Statistical design of Path to Prevention platform trial in early neuronal alpha-synuclein disease
abstract: The Path to Prevention (P2P) platform trial is a first-in-class, phase 2A, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled learning study. Its design expedites the assessment of investigational therapies for the treatment of early-stage Neuronal α-Synuclein Disease (NSD), a biological disease continuum that encompasses and often precedes clinically manifest Parkinson’s Disease. P2P is embedded within the Parkinson’s Precision Medicine Initiative (PPMI), a robust observational longitudinal cohort study on Parkinson’s disease progression and a trial-facilitating enrollment framework. A regimen , comprised of an active investigational therapy and a matched placebo control, evaluates a therapeutic candidate within the P2P perpetual platform framework. Multiple regimens can be enrolled, enabling efficient testing of multiple therapeutics. A two-stage randomization scheme determines regimen sample size with 125 participants assigned to a regimen’s active therapy and a variable number to placebo control. The treated follow up period is a minimum of 96 weeks and a maximum of 144 weeks, with the last randomized participant followed for 96 weeks. As a pioneering interventional trial in early-stage NSD, P2P endpoint selection was critically informed by modeling and analysis of available PPMI data. In P2P, regimens will be evaluated for efficacy using two primary endpoints: 1) a biomarker outcome of Dopamine Transporter Single-Photon Emission Computed Tomography (DAT SPECT) imaging measured by the bilateral putamen Specific Binding Ratio (SBR) and 2) a clinical outcome measured by the Movement Disorder Society-Sponsored Revision of the Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS) Part III score. Each endpoint will be assessed separately using a longitudinal Bayesian mixed effects model, which compares the active treatment group to the shared placebo control group. The model uses regimen-specific controls at full weight and dynamically discounts controls from other regimens. Additionally, placebo control estimates are supplemented by non-randomized control data from the PPMI cohort. Clinical trial simulations, informed by longitudinal data from 275 P2P-eligible PPMI study participants (Age 60-81, 35% Female, 65% Male), were conducted to evaluate the design. Each regimen is well-powered to detect a 40% slowing in progression for both the clinical and biomarker primary endpoints when comparing active treatment to randomized control data. Supplementing the control estimation with non-randomized, P2P-eligible registry participant data increases power in the explored scenarios up to 4% for each endpoint. The embedded P2P platform trial is a powerful learning study that leverages statistical efficiencies from the platform trial design and established PPMI infrastructure and is poised to advance treatment development in early-stage NSD.

title: Personalized Prediction of Differences in fMRI Connectivity Estimates Across Preprocessing Pipelines
abstract: Longitudinal functional MRI of the human brain is valuable for tracking changes in functional connectivity (FC) associated with disease progression or treatment response. Even so, measured FC values depend on preprocessing, and nuisance regression and temporal filtering affect individuals differently. We examined whether we could use earlier scans to predict how preprocessing would affect a later scan. In 69 ADNI (Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative) participants scanned three times, we measured how nuisance regression and filtering, alone and in sequence, changed the measured FC. A ridge regression model combined these responses with baseline FC from the third scan to predict the effect of reversing the processing order. Just four coefficients were shared across 79,800 connections. In leave-one-participant-out testing, mean squared error was 0.012, compared with 0.017 for predicting the same average response for everyone. It outperformed the best of seven alternative predictions chosen for each participant (0.013; normalized gain 0.069, 95% bootstrap interval 0.006–0.134), with lower error in 44 of 69 participants. About half the benefit of using each person’s earlier responses, rather than the average across participants, came from which connections changed. This advantage persisted after accounting for acquisition variables. The ADNI-trained model reduced mean error in ten Midnight Scan Club participants without refitting. These results support using personal preprocessing history to predict changes in connectivity estimates on newly acquired scans.

title: Cross-cancer knowledge transfer for lymph node metastasis prediction: Applicability of an axillary lymph node-based deep learning model
abstract: Evaluation of lymph node (LN) metastasis is critical for cancer staging and treatment planning. Since radiologic hallmarks of metastatic LNs are shared across primary cancers, a computed tomography (CT)-based deep learning (DL) classifier developed from one anatomy may transfer to others. This study built a DenseNet-121 ensemble model using clinical-implication-applied preprocessing and evaluated its cross-anatomical generalizability to LNs from diverse primary cancers. A DenseNet-121 ensemble model combining fixed-size cropping (FSC) and adjustable square cropping (ASC) was trained from ImageNet initialization on an axillary lymph node (ALN) dataset (n = 1,128 from 523 breast cancer patients). The model utilized clinical-implication-applied perinodal cropping with bicubic filtering and standardized resizing. To test cross-anatomical generalizability, an external dataset of 256 CT images across four anatomical regions was evaluated: cervical, mediastinal, upper-abdominal, and lower-abdominal LNs. Perinodal free margins were systematically varied from 10% to 40% to optimize the balance between context preservation and surround interference. Bicubic filtering and standardized resizing yielded the highest internal performance on the original ALN dataset (FSC-ASC ensemble area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC] 0.958, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.920–0.987 at 40% margin). The model demonstrated site-dependent, above-chance generalizability across all external regions. Cervical LNs achieved the highest performance at a 40% margin (AUROC 0.939, 95% CI 0.875–0.989). Mediastinal LNs peaked at a 10% margin (AUROC 0.796, 95% CI 0.672–0.903), with wider margins degrading performance due to adjacent structural interference. Upper-abdominal and lower-abdominal LNs reached optimal performance at a 30% margin (AUROC 0.814 for upper; AUROC 0.917 for lower). A single ALN-trained DL model can accurately predict LN metastasis across cervical, mediastinal, and abdominal stations through site-specific perinodal margin tuning. These findings support the feasibility of cross-cancer knowledge transfer and the clinical utility of generalizable backbones for pan-cancer nodal assessment.

title: Disability-relevant demyelination in multiple sclerosis: five-year evolution following diagnosis
abstract: Improved understanding of how myelin damage contributes to disability in multiple sclerosis (MS) is needed to inform targeted therapeutic strategies and improve clinical trial platforms. Magnetization transfer saturation (MTsat) and T1 relaxometry provide in vivo quantitative MRI measures of myelin integrity, and may offer insights into disability-relevant pathology beyond inflammatory relapse. This longitudinal study explores the relationship between early demyelination and disability progression over the first five years following diagnosis. 62 people with relapsing-remitting (pwRR)MS ([≤] 6 months post-diagnosis, 48 female, mean age 38 years) underwent baseline and one-year MRI and Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) assessment. At five-year follow-up, 56/62 (90.3%) completed EDSS and 40/62 additionally completed MRI (64.5%). Disability progression was defined as an increase of [≥] 1.5, [≥] 1.0 or [≥] 0.5 points for a previous EDSS score of < 1.0, 1.0 to 5.5, and [≥] 6.0, respectively. Baseline neurofilament light chain (NfL), glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), and EBNA1 immunoglobulin (IgG) titres were also measured. MTsat was calculated within normal-appearing white matter (NAWM), white matter lesions (WML), cortical and deep grey matter (GM) structures. Associations between change in MTsat and disability progression were assessed with binomial logistic regression. Interactions with interval disease activity (i.e. new/enlarging lesions [NELs]) were investigated, and comparisons were made with healthy control test-retest data (n = 11). Exploratory analyses were performed for: (prolonged) T1; baseline metrics; blood-derived markers; diffusion-weighted imaging; and, disability-associated differences in five-year microstructural MRI trajectories. Greater baseline-to-one-year decreases in NAWM and WML MTsat were associated with baseline-to-one-year disability progression (adjusted odds ratio [95% confidence interval] = 0.255 [0.078 to 0.602] and 0.261 [0.084 to 0.638]; false discovery rate [FDR]-corrected p-value = 0.015 and 0.015). NELs did not influence these associations (interaction p-values > 0.05). One-to-five-year changes in MTsat were not associated with one-to-five-year disability progression (FDR-corrected p-values > 0.05). Neither baseline nor baseline-to-one-year MTsat changes predicted future disability progression. No exploratory analyses reached FDR-corrected statistical significance. We show for the first time that progressive NAWM and WML demyelination measured with MTsat is associated with early disability progression in recently diagnosed RRMS, independent of radiological inflammatory disease activity. Neither MTsat nor T1 are associated with longer-term progression over the subsequent four years. MTsat is sensitive to disability-relevant demyelination not visible on conventional MRI, indicates a potential early window of therapeutic opportunity in the year following diagnosis, and is a promising clinically applicable disease stratifier and surrogate endpoint for therapeutic trials.

title: Agentic AI enables cell segmentation-free cell-type inference and cell-type-guided cell segmentation in spatial transcriptomics
abstract: Cell-type identification in spatial transcriptomics often relies on cell segmentation, which can introduce inaccuracies in cell boundaries and transcript assignment. Segmentation-free or cell-free methods have been developed to completely avoid cell segmentation, but inaccurate cell typing hinder accurate downstream analysis. Here, we introduce SSAF-T, a segmentation-free agentic framework that identifies cell types directly from spatial gene expression without predefined reference datasets. For the reference-free cell typing, SSAF-T incorporates CeLLMan, which employs expert-level agents for each organ to annotate cell types using a literature-grounded knowledge graph. We benchmark SSAF-T on both array-based and imaging-based spatial transcriptomics datasets in terms of accuracy, reproducibility, and scalability. We further show that SSAF-T provides an accurate cell segmentation based on the segmentation-free mapping, which ensure compatibility to existing downstream analysis ecosystem, and eventually enable quantitative analysis at single-cell level.

title: Benchmarking foundation models for resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging time series in cognitive aging research
abstract: Foundation models trained on large neuroimaging datasets could help smaller studies investigate cognition from brain recordings. However, whether the foundation model-derived representations improve assessment of current cognition, prediction of follow-up cognition, or characterization of cognitive change remains unclear. We evaluated nine configurations from five model families that process regional resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging time series, using 3,103 scans from 1,653 participants across two observational and five intervention aging cohorts. Primary frozen representations showed no consistent superiority over conventional functional connectivity for concurrent cognitive associations or diagnostic classification. Changing the readout improved selected concurrent cognitive associations without updating model weights, indicating that performance depended partly on how representations were extracted. Additional post-training and embedding alignment yielded gains in selected settings but did not consistently improve performance across outcomes. In the primary longitudinal analyses, imaging representations did not establish added value beyond baseline clinical measures. These findings show that readout choice influences concurrent cognitive associations, while the added value of these representations for longitudinal outcomes remains unestablished.

title: Computational Modeling of the Acoustic Radiation Force and Viscoelastic Displacement for Transcranial Focused Ultrasound Neuromodulation
abstract: Objective In transcranial ultrasound neuromodulation (TUS), simulations of the harmonic pressure are often used for treatment planning. However, other mechanisms of energy transfer, such as acoustic radiation force (ARF) and the resulting tissue displacement, are reported less frequently. Furthermore, there is limited guidance on how these mechanisms should be simulated. This study evaluates the numerical convergence and accuracy of different ARF formulations and investigates the simulation of ultrasound-induced tissue displacement in the context of TUS. Approach Two simulations steps are used in k-Wave to first simulate the first order acoustic pressure and velocity fields. Subsequently, these fields are used to calculate the ARF using the momentum-flux density tensor, Reynold’s stress force, and attenuation force formulations. The ARF is then applied as input for a second viscoelastic simulation to estimate the tissue displacement induced by the ultrasound field. Numerical accuracy and convergence are quantified as functions of the various numerical choices and hyperparameters in the solvers. Main results Among the investigated formulations, the attenuation-force approach proved to be the most robust and the least susceptible to numerical errors across variable medium types and transducer geometries. Within the parameter space relevant to TUS, it is a valid approximation of the momentum flux density tensor formulation. Similar tissue displacement distributions are found across the different ARF formulations. However, the accuracy of the displacement simulation decreases with increasing pulse duration. Finally, recommendations are formulated on the ARF calculation method and on the numerical hyperparameters for ARF and displacement simulations. Significance This study offers guidelines for calculating the ARF and simulating tissue displacement. The proposed framework enables a more comprehensive characterization of ultrasound-mediated energy transfer in TUS.

title: Redefining Synovial Pathotypes in Psoriatic Arthritis through Multi-Modal Histology and Machine Learning (The PSYNOVIUM Study)
abstract: Background Synovial inflammation in psoriatic arthritis (PsA) lacks a validated histological classification framework. Current approaches apply rheumatoid arthritis (RA) synovial pathotypes to PsA, which overlooks immunobiological differences between the diseases and limits the predictive power of tissue stratification. We aimed to define data-driven, PsA-specific synovial pathotypes to facilitate tissue-driven precision medicine. Methods In this cross-sectional study, ultrasound-guided synovial biopsies were obtained from 61 patients with PsA (n=22), seropositive RA (n=23), seronegative RA (n=10), and other inflammatory arthritides (n=6). Sections underwent multi-modal staining, including H&E, picrosirius red, and immunohisto-chemistry for CD3, CD20, CD68, CD138, and CD31. title: Preprocessing Determines Whether Fractal Biomarkers Detect Neurodegeneration: A Systematic Evaluation Across Five fMRI Pipelines
abstract: Fractal analysis of resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) has been proposed for detecting altered neural dynamics in Alzheimer’s disease (AD), but the effect of preprocessing on these measurements is poorly constrained. We evaluated 229 ADNI3 participants (156 cognitively normal [CN], 60 mild cognitive impairment [MCI], and 13 AD) processed with five ENIGMA HALFpipe variants. Each scan contained 197 volumes (TR = 3.0 s) and 434 regional time series. The reported CN–AD effect varied 4.5-fold for the detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA) Hurst exponent and 13.1-fold for Sample Entropy; both measures met p < 0.05 only after aCompCor. Under aCompCor, mean H was 0.812 in CN, 0.827 in MCI, and 0.872 in AD (d = −1.40, p = 0.0003), whereas the other four DFA effects were approximately d = −0.31 to −0.40. A variance decomposition attributed 41.5% of total H variance to pipeline, 44.5% to participant, and 0.3% to diagnosis. Whole-brain analysis found higher H in AD across 16 of 18 networks, with 36 cortical regions surviving false-discovery-rate correction. Synthetic fractional Gaussian noise experiments confirmed monotonic DFA estimation at the available scan length. The small AD group makes all disease-effect estimates exploratory. These results show that preprocessing choice can determine whether fractal group differences are detectable and should therefore be treated as part of the biomarker definition.

title: Identification of Kinome Biomarkers and Therapeutic Rescue in cGMP-Linked Retinal Degeneration
abstract: Inherited retinal degenerations, such as Retinitis Pigmentosa (RP) and Leber’s congenital amaurosis (LCA), are major causes of progressive and irreversible vision loss. The large number of genes associated with these disorders makes their clinical and molecular characterization difficult, while systemic biomarkers for disease progression or treatment response remain limited. These challenges were addressed by targeting cGMP-associated mechanisms shared by RP and LCA and integrating systemic biomarker profiling with retinal outcomes. Kinase activity analysis (kinome analysis) in peripheral blood mononuclear cells distinguished healthy and diseased states and captured therapy-associated signatures in rd10 mice treated with LP-CN03, a liposomal formulation of the cGMP analog CN03. This first systemic analysis in a therapeutically responsive animal model highlights kinome analysis as a potential translational readout. Given shared cGMP signaling in RP and AIPL1 -associated LCA, LP-CN03’s therapeutic potential was further evaluated in a new CRISPR-Cas9-generated Aipl1 ⁻/⁻ mouse model. Treatment with LP-CN03 preserved retinal structure and function, as shown by electroretinography, longitudinal optical coherence tomography, fundus imaging, optomotor testing, and photoreceptor-specific gene expression. Together, these findings provide independent in vivo evidence for the neuroprotective effect of LP-CN03 in both cGMP-related RP and LCA, also highlighting the translational value of kinome profiling. title: Mapping the brain-web morphology to characterise ageing and cognitive impairment
abstract: Ageing reshapes human brain anatomy across spatial scales, yet its geometrical organisation remains difficult to quantify. Here we introduce SHARP (Spectral Hierarchy Analysis, Reconstruction and Prediction), which transfers hierarchical cosmic-web classification to structural MRI, identifying knots, filaments, sheets and voids at four spectral levels and combining their morphology with higher-order spatial statistics and anatomical measurements. In CamCAN , selected filament- and sheet-associated features show opposing correlations with age and distinct associations with subcortical and ventricular volumes. To quantify their contribution, we compare SHARP with a neural-network baseline combining 36 regional anatomical measurements, total brain volume and sex. Adding cosmologically motivated descriptors reduces the mean absolute error of MRI-only age prediction from 6.04 to 4.71 years (22%) in CamCAN and from 4.57 to 4.07 years (11%) in OASIS-3 under participant-independent validation. Brain-web morphology with only brain volume and sex already achieves 5.12 years in CamCAN . For cognitive-status classification in OASIS-3, SHARP identifies 85% of Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR)-positive observations at 86% specificity, compared with 78% sensitivity for the anatomical baseline at matched empirical specificity. These results demonstrate that cosmological methods provide complementary geometrical information and measurable gains in characterising brain ageing and cognitive impairment.

title: Accessing Mesoscale Functional Organization from Standard Functional MRI Leveraging AI-Based Super-Resolution
abstract: Access to the fine-scale functional organization of the human brain is essential for understanding cognition and neurological disorders yet remains beyond the reach of conventional functional MRI (fMRI) because of its limited spatial resolution and contrast-to-noise ratio. To overcome this limitation, we developed f-LENNS (functional Localization Enhancement via Neural-Net-Sharpening), an artificial intelligence (AI)-based framework that enhances the effective spatial resolution of reconstructed fMRI magnitude images. The model was trained exclusively on high-resolution synthetic MRI data using extensive domain randomization and no adversarial or generative components. This approach enables robust out-of-the-box generalization (without retraining) to experimental datasets obtained with diverse acquisitions, while effectively curbing hallucination. Our experiments show that our publicly available model substantially improves the spatial fidelity of functional activation maps across multiple imaging paradigms and generalizes to a cohort of individuals with atypical brain function caused by amblyopia (lazy eye). F-LENNS consistently outperforms conventional resolution enhancement approaches, including interpolation-based upsampling and sharpening methods. These findings demonstrate that AI-driven super-resolution combined with domain randomization can overcome domain shifts arising from differences in MRI acquisition, enabling scalable, fine-scale functional brain mapping with widely available MRI hardware. Summary statement Precision functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) at the mesoscale is transforming our understanding of human brain functions by enabling the visualization of fine-grained functional organization in the human brain. Recent advances have shown that precision fMRI can reveal heterogeneous cortical architecture, resolve mesoscale processing streams underlying sensory perception, attention, and decision-making, identify functional alterations associated with neurological disorders, and help explain inter-individual variability in cognition. However, the widespread adoption of these approaches remains constrained by the limited availability of ultra-high-field MRI systems. Here, we introduce f-LENNS (functional Localization Enhancement via Neural-Net Sharpening), an artificial intelligence (AI)-based framework that broadens access to mesoscale functional neuroimaging by enhancing the effective spatial resolution of conventional fMRI. The model is trained exclusively on domain-randomized synthetic MRI data and generalizes to diverse datasets without retraining : f-LENNS can super-resolve data obtained with different acquisition parameters and at different magnetic field strengths (3T and 7T), while minimizing hallucination artifacts. F-LENNS substantially improves the detectability and spatial fidelity of fine-scale functional organization defined by stimulus-evoked activity and accurately recovers mesoscale functional patterns from conventional-resolution fMRI. Importantly, the same model generalizes to individuals with atypical brain function, revealing disorder-related functional abnormalities without data- or disease-specific retraining. Together, these findings demonstrate that domain randomization enables AI-based super-resolution models to overcome domain shifts arising from heterogeneous MRI hardware and acquisition protocols. Compared with conventional approaches, including interpolation-based upsampling, AFNI sharpening, and AI models trained on real functional and/or structural MRI data, f-LENNS consistently provides superior reconstruction of fine-scale functional organization. By enabling precision functional imaging in individual participants using widely available MRI systems, f-LENNS expands access to mesoscale brain mapping and represents an important step toward scalable, individualized functional neuroimaging and precision medicine.

title: Automated MRI-Based Segmentation of the Cranio-Cervical Venous System Using a Dedicated Deep Learning Pipeline
abstract: ABSTRACT PURPOSE To develop an automated magnetic resonance imaging based segmentation pipeline for the cranio-cervical venous system (CCVS), a complex anatomical network for which no dedicated segmentation tool is currently available. MATERIALS AND METHODS A retrospective single-center cohort of 194 contrast-enhanced cranio-cervical MRI examinations acquired between 2019 and 2024 was used. Manual reference segmentations were initially performed on 50 examinations using 3D Slicer. A nnU-Net v2-based segmentation model was then trained through an iterative process combining automatic segmentation, manual correction, and retraining. A dedicated intermediate model was developed to distinguish the vertebral artery from the surrounding vertebral venous plexus. Segmentation performance was assessed using the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC). The complete processing pipeline was integrated into an open-source software application, VenousNetworkAnalyzer (VNA). RESULTS The final model achieved a mean DSC of 0.94 (95% CI, 0.93–0.95) in five-fold cross-validation on 106 examinations with manual reference segmentations. Iterative optimization progressively reduced manual processing time from approximately 10 hours of fully manual segmentation to less than 10 minutes of manual correction per patient. Application of the final model to the entire cohort enabled the generation of patient-specific three-dimensional reconstructions of the cranio-cervical venous system. The segmentation workflow was successfully integrated into the VNA software environment, allowing automated processing and visualization of MRI datasets. CONCLUSION This study demonstrates the feasibility of automated segmentation of the cranio-cervical venous system from contrast-enhanced MRI using a dedicated deep-learning pipeline. The resulting reduction in processing time and integration into an open-source software platform provide a foundation for future large-scale anatomical studies of cranio-cervical venous drainage. Summary Statement An automated nnU-Net-based MRI pipeline enabled segmentation and three-dimensional visualization of the cranio-cervical venous system, reducing manual correction time less than 10 minutes per case. Key Points - A dedicated nnU-Net v2-based pipeline was developed for MRI-based segmentation of the cranio-cervical venous system - Iterative model optimization reduced manual processing time from approximately 10 hours to less than 10 minutes per case. - The pipeline enabled patient-specific three-dimensional reconstructions and was integrated into a dedicated software environment for visualization and analyzis.

title: MLX-Radiomics: accelerating standardized regional and voxel-wise radiomics for CT, PET and MRI
abstract: BackgroundDifferences among radiomics implementations complicate cross-study comparisons, while voxel-wise feature extraction remains computationally demanding. We developed MLX-Radiomics to accelerate regional feature extraction and voxel-wise mapping while preserving agreement with standardized reference measurements. MethodsMLX-Radiomics implements 172 feature definitions from the Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative (IBSI), 16 extensions and the IBSI 2 image filters. We assessed agreement with IBSI reference data and evaluated numerical accuracy against independent double-precision and analytic calculations. In matched comparisons on Apple M1 Max and M5 Max systems, we used the IBSI reference CT to compare feature values, extraction time and memory use with PyRadiomics, MIRP and Flash-Radiomics, and feature values with FastRad. Separately, we compared the time required to generate voxel-wise feature maps for regions of up to 10.1 million voxels with published GPU results obtained on different hardware and images. We evaluated agreement with MIRP under published settings in a 51-patient cohort with CT, FDG PET and T1-weighted MRI. ResultsMLX-Radiomics agreed with all 2,160 IBSI reference measurements within the specified tolerances. With matching outputs, MLX-Radiomics was 2.66 to 7.27 times faster than PyRadiomics and MIRP for regional feature extraction and 198 to 218 times faster than PyRadiomics for voxel-wise mapping on a 243-voxel crop. It also outperformed the fastest Flash-Radiomics CPU configurations tested. On the M5 Max, generating 93 maps over 10.1 million voxels took 23.8 s. In the patient cohort, MLX-Radiomics and MIRP agreed on 98.0% of requested values. For tumors at the image edge, matching the libraries resampling rules substantially improved agreement. ConclusionsMLX-Radiomics provides standardized regional measurements and voxel-wise maps for CT, PET and MRI, with evidence of faster extraction limited to CT. It can support quantitative imaging research on relatively inexpensive hardware without requiring a separate GPU workstation.

title: OmniT2I: a unified table-to-image framework for survival prediction and cross-modal inference with incomplete multimodal cancer data
abstract: Molecular profiles and histopathology provide complementary information about cancer prognosis, but these data are often incomplete for individual patients. Here we present OmniT2I, a table-to-image framework for survival prediction and cross-modal inference from incomplete multimodal cancer data. Each molecular profile was converted into a three-channel image representation with correlation-based feature placement. OmniT2I combines available molecular and histopathology embeddings through availability-aware fusion and predicts missing modalities from those observed. Across 10,373 patients with 32 cancer types, the C-index was 0.631 within cancer types and 0.783 with all cancers pooled (0.660 and 0.787 in 5,605 patients with all five modalities). A single model handled all 31 modality combinations and, compared with nine survival methods trained separately for each, achieved higher C-indices in 240 of 279 pooled and 226 of 279 within-cancer comparisons. Adding predictions of withheld modalities to observed inputs improved pooled C-indices in all 180 pairings of observed and withheld modality sets and within-cancer C-indices in 164. Adding measured histopathology to RNA produced the largest within-cancer C-index gain among the four additional modalities evaluated, whereas adding copy number variation reduced it. In seven external cohorts, frozen RNA-only C-indices differed from test performance in the corresponding cancer type in TCGA by a median of −0.003 (range, −0.092 to +0.079). OmniT2I enables prognostic modeling with incomplete multimodal data.

title: WALRUS: Robust and Transferable Deep Learning for Water and Lipid Removal in 1H-MRSI
abstract: Proton magnetic resonance spectroscopic imaging (1H-MRSI) enables non-invasive mapping of brain metabolism, but reliable quantification is challenged by residual water and extracranial lipid contamination. Recent work demonstrated that a deep learning model trained on simulated metabolite spectra combined with in vivo-derived water and lipid signals can outperform conventional nuisance-removal methods. However, this approach relied on heuristic simulation parameter distributions and a subject-specific L2-derived lipid estimate as an auxiliary network input, requiring subject-specific lipid masks and L2 processing during inference. Here, we introduce WALRUS (Water And Lipid Removal Using Spectral Learning), a fitting-consistent and empirically calibrated framework developed through a systematic evaluation of simulation realism, architectural priors, and network optimization. WALRUS uses the same metabolite basis as downstream spectral fitting and calibrates deliberately broadened simulation distributions from in vivo measurements. Controlled 7 T experiments demonstrate that empirical simulator calibration substantially improves nuisance removal and metabolite quantification compared with heuristic training distributions. With the optimized simulator, a capacity-matched comparison reveals no clear additional benefit from the L2-derived prior, allowing its removal and substantially simplifying inference. Further improvements are achieved with the final higher-capacity U-Net, while on-the-fly simulation improves generalization compared with training on a fixed synthetic dataset. The same framework was subsequently recalibrated and retrained at 3 T, where WALRUS outperformed conventional HLSVD+L2 processing on held-out data. Together, WALRUS combines these advances into an optimized framework that improves nuisance removal and downstream metabolite fitting, requires no subject-specific lipid segmentation or L2-derived auxiliary input during inference, and can be systematically adapted to different acquisition settings.

title: Large Language Models to Label CT Radiology Reports for Incidental Findings Found in Lung Cancer Screening: A Comparative Analysis
abstract: ObjectiveTo compare LLM and prompting strategies for labeling Specific Incidental Findings (SIFs) occurring during lung cancer screening, in radiology reports. Materials and MethodsIn this retrospective study, 300 CT reports from a Dutch academic hospital were included between 19th March 2003 and 28th December 2020. GPT-5, GPT-4-Turbo, Llama-3.1-8B-INST, MedGemma-4B-IT, a keyword-based search method, and a radiologist labelled the reports for the presence or absence of nine SIFs. The radiologists scores were the reference standard. Each LLM was evaluated with four different prompting strategies: two without Chain-of-Thought (CoT), and two with CoT (one zero shot, one few shot). The automated labelling methods were evaluated against the radiologist primarily using Cohens Kappa, and additionally sensitivity, specificity, and F1 scores. ResultsGPT-5 achieved substantial or almost perfect agreement for seven out of nine SIFs: aortic valve disease, bronchiectasis, consolidation, coronary artery calcification, emphysema, abnormality in mediastinal lymph nodes, and thyroid abnormalities, with Cohen {kappa} values of 0.81 (0.70, 0.93), 0.97 (0.93, 1.00), 0.71 (0.62, 0.82), 0.92 (0.87, 0.96), 0.91 (0.84, 0.97), 0.71 (0.62, 0.80), and 0.92 (0.86, 0.98) respectively. For the remaining two SIFs, moderate LLM agreement was obtained with MedGemma-4B-IT and with GPT-4-Turbo with Cohen {kappa} values of 0.48 (0.40, 0.60), 0.42 (0.31, 0.58) for interstitial lung abnormalities and mediastinal mass respectively. The highest agreement was obtained with the non-CoT prompt strategies for most SIFs. ConclusionThis study demonstrated that LLMs can automatically label radiology reports with agreement ranging from almost perfect to moderate, but not one LLM - prompt combination achieved the highest agreement across all SIFs.

title: Cortical brain changes from early to mid-adolescence in offspring at familial high risk for schizophrenia or bipolar disorder
abstract: Objective: Schizophrenia (SZ) and bipolar disorder (BP) emerge in late adolescence or adulthood. Offspring at familial high risk for SZ (FHR-SZ) or BP (FHR-BP) are more likely to develop psychiatric disorders. Prior work from the Danish High Risk and Resilience (VIA) Study found sex-specific volumetric brain differences in offspring at FHR-SZ and FHR-BP aged 11-12 years. This study builds upon these findings by testing whether they reflect group differences in rate of change or stable group differences from early to mid-adolescence. Methods: This study investigated MRI data from offspring at FHR-SZ, FHR-BP, and population- based controls (PBC) at baseline (11-12 years; n=288) and follow-up (15-16 years; n=249). FreeSurfer longitudinal processing derived total brain volume, cortical measures, and intracranial volume (ICV). Linear mixed-effects models tested group-by-age interactions and sex-specific group effects, as well as associations with psychotic experiences (PE) and lifetime Axis-I mental disorders. Results: The analysis did not detect group-by-age interactions, indicating similar developmental slopes across groups. However, at both time points, males at FHR-SZ demonstrated reduced brain and cortical volumes compared to PBC and FHR-BP males. These effects were attenuated after adjusting for ICV, which was reduced in males at FHR-SZ. The analysis additionally detected volumetric reductions in males with PE, after controlling for risk status. Conclusions: These results extend the previous findings to ages 15-16 years, indicating group differences are stable and persist into mid-adolescence. Associations with ICV suggest early neurodevelopmental effects, and volumetric reductions in males with PE suggest convergent effects with FHR-SZ.

title: Lamina Cribrosa Strain as a Glaucoma Prognostic Factor: The STRAIN Study Methodology and Initial Outcomes
abstract: Objective To estimate the lamina cribrosa (LC) strain response to intraocular pressure (IOP) change in open angle glaucoma (OAG) patients and examine associations between LC strain and demographic and clinical characteristics relevant to OAG in an ongoing longitudinal study. Design Cohort study Participants Adult patients with OAG (205 eyes of 119 patients) Methods The STRAIN study is an ongoing longitudinal study designed to determine whether LC biomechanical strain is associated with present, prior, and future OAG damage. In this initial analysis, patients either temporarily stopped ≥1 eye drop, initiated an eye drop, or underwent selective laser trabeculoplasty to produce IOP change. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) scans of the optic nerve head (ONH) acquired before and up to several weeks after IOP change were analyzed using digital volume correlation (DVC) to estimate LC strain. Strain measurements were compared with age, race, sex, axial length, central corneal thickness (CCT), corneal hysteresis, optic disc area, years of known OAG, retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thickness, and visual field mean deviation (MD). Main Outcome Measures LC strain estimated by DVC from OCT scans acquired before and after IOP alteration. Results Axial LC strain ( Ezz ) was tensile with IOP decrease and compressive with IOP increase. Maximum principal strain was tensile (mean E max = 1.09%), and maximum shear strain was positive (mean Γ max = 1.16%) in the radial-axial plane. Both increased quadratically with the IOP change. Older age was significantly related to greater tensile circumferential strain ( p = 0.02) and lower Γ max ( p = 0.01). Sex, CCT, corneal hysteresis, and optic disc area were not significantly associated with LC strain. In combined multivariable models adjusting for IOP change, demographics, and accounting for correlations between eyes from the same patient, eyes with thinner inferior-quadrant RNFL had smaller Γ max for a given IOP change ( p = 0.02). Conclusions LC strain in patients with OAG is associated with the degree of neuronal loss, age, and axial length, supporting a relationship between the LC biomechanical response and factors relevant to glaucomatous damage.

title: LungAI: An AI Biomarker that Refines Lung-RADS v2022 Triage of Screen-Detected Pulmonary Nodules
abstract: BackgroundThe Lung-RADS algorithm standardizes the management of screen-detected pulmonary nodules, but its risk assessment is driven chiefly by nodule size and attenuation. This misallocates a meaningful fraction of patients: a nontrivial share of small malignancies receive 12-month surveillance while large benign nodules proceed to invasive workup. Artificial intelligence (AI) may supply risk information independent of the imaging features Lung-RADS already uses. MethodsWe validated LungAI, an investigational deep learning nodule malignancy classifier not yet cleared by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), on the held-out NLST test partition of Ardila et al. (2,747 low-dose CT examinations from 1,244 patients with [≥]1 solid or part-solid 4-30 mm nodule; 89 pathologically confirmed cancers, prevalence 3.2%). We compared discrimination against Sybil, mean nodule diameter, and estimated nodule volume. A board-certified radiologist assigned Lung-RADS v2022 categories to a positives-enriched random subset (226 eligible examinations; 78 cancers), projected to the full cohort by contingency weighting. A per-category reclassification algorithm shifted patients along the existing Lung-RADS management ladder using a-priori score cutpoints. We evaluated a separately locked follow-up configuration on examinations with a prior scan. ResultsLungAI achieved AUROC 0.92 (95% CI 0.88-0.95) and AUPRC 0.47 (0.35-0.61), outperforming Sybil ({Delta}AUROC 0.07; {Delta}AUPRC 0.18), diameter ({Delta}AUROC 0.14; {Delta}AUPRC 0.34), and volume ({Delta}AUROC 0.14; {Delta}AUPRC 0.38; all P<0.001). Against Lung-RADS v2022 scored ordinally on the weighted annotated subset, LungAI improved AUPRC ({Delta}AUPRC 0.31, P=0.003) but not AUROC ({Delta}AUROC 0.03, P=0.20). LungAI added discriminative information independent of diameter (likelihood-ratio {chi}2=161, P<10-36; {Delta}AUROC 0.10) and, on follow-up examinations, independent of delta diameter, volume doubling time, and new-nodule status ({chi}2=79, P<10-18). Integrated with Lung-RADS, LungAI reduced cancers on the slowest (12-month rescan) pathway by 46% (3.1[->]1.6 per 1,000 examinations) and benign biopsy referrals by 20% (32.7[->]26.2 per 1,000 examinations) at approximately unchanged total biopsy volume (51.0[->]50.1 per 1,000). Assuming full adherence to recommended follow-up, the combined approach yielded 25 months of net diagnostic lead time, an estimated net cost saving of [~]$2,200, and 6.5 fewer benign biopsies per 1,000 examinations; accounting for published adherence rates, it yielded 1.6 additional cancer diagnoses within 1 year per 1,000 examinations. ConclusionsLungAI contributes malignancy-risk information orthogonal to the size- and growth-based features underlying Lung-RADS and improves the allocation of screening patients across the existing management spectrum while potentially decreasing invasive procedures for benign lesions. Multi-site, multi-geography validation is required to demonstrate practical generalizability.

title: Beyond organ age gaps: comparing plasma proteomic metrics of organ biology in relation to brain structure and neurodegenerative disease
abstract: Biological aging is heterogeneous across organ systems, and brain health may be influenced by biological processes extending beyond the central nervous system (CNS). This can be investigated using biological age measures that are increasingly used to estimate how biological systems deviate from chronological aging. However, organ level plasma proteomic metrics may capture different forms of biological variation depending on how they are defined. Here, we compared three complementary organ level proteomic metrics across 15 organ systems (and two global systems) in relation to age, organ-relevant physiological phenotypes, brain morphometry, and incident neurodegenerative disease, using plasma proteomics from 52,667 UK Biobank participants and brain MRI data from 5,078 of those individuals. We derived i) supervised age gap metrics using XGBoost models trained to predict chronological age, ii) unsupervised PC1 metrics capturing dominant organ-associated proteomic variation, and iii) phenotype guided PLS metrics linking plasma proteins to organ-relevant physiological traits. The three metric classes were related but not interchangeable. Global all-protein and all-organ-protein models showed strong age-related proteomic structure. However, organ-specific PC analyses showed that age was often but not always the dominant source of variation in protein signal across organs. Age gap metrics showed the most consistent associations with subsequent ICD-10based neurodegenerative and vascular diagnoses, whereas all three metric classes showed distinct associations with brain structure and organ-relevant physiological phenotypes. Brain structure analyses revealed heterogeneous organ–brain association patterns across organs, suggesting that proteomic variation relates to brain structure in both a systemic and an organ-specific manner. Several systemic and organ-specific signals partially mediated the associations between disease specific genetic risk and incident diagnoses of Alzheimer’s disease and stroke, albeit with small effect sizes (1-8%). Similarly, organ metrics provided modest incremental predictive improvement over baseline demographic models, with the largest increase in ROC-AUC observed for Alzheimer’s disease when all organ age gap metrics were added jointly (ΔROC-AUC = 0.037). These results link brain related outcomes to proteomic variation across both CNS and non-CNS systems. Our work suggests that proteomic organ metrics capture complementary dimensions of biological variation rather than a single construct of organ aging. Although these measures may provide informative biological and potentially predictive signals, their incremental predictive value in the present analyses was modest.

title: Volumetric Analysis of the Deltoid Muscle From Neck-to-Knee Dixon MRI: A pilot population assessment of a posterior intramuscular injection target
abstract: BackgroundDeltoid muscle volume varies across anatomical regions and population groups, with potential implications for intramuscular injection site selection. Evidence comparing middle and posterior deltoid volumes in vaccine-eligible populations is limited. PurposeTo compare middle and posterior deltoid muscle volumes by vaccine eligibility group, sex, and side. MethodsDeltoid muscles were manually segmented into anterior, middle and posterior regions in 43 UK Biobank Dixon MRI scans. A MONAI deep learning model trained on the annotations (Dice score = 0.78) segmented deltoid muscles of 5,239 participants, categorised by UK flu vaccination eligibility: A ([≥]65 years without risk conditions, n=1,760), B ([≥]65 with risk conditions, n=1,744), and C (<65 with risk conditions, n=1,735). Bilateral-average posterior and middle volumes were compared using a paired t-test. A linear mixed-effects model assessed posterior-middle differences by group, sex and side. ResultsMean age was 66.7 {+/-} 7.2 years and body mass index was 27.5 {+/-} 5.7 kg/m2 (mean {+/-} SD). Posterior deltoid volume exceeded the middle deltoid volume by 55.36 ml (95% CI, 54.14-56.58, p<0.0001). Posterior-middle differences were largest in Group A, followed by B and then C, greater in men, and greater on the right side (all p<0.0001). Mean segmentation-quality score was 4.27 {+/-} 0.73 on a five-point Likert scale and weighted inter-observer kappa was 0.583 (95% CI, 0.452 - 0.713). ConclusionsAmong individuals eligible for the UK flu immunisation, posterior deltoid volume was greater than middle deltoid volume. These findings support further anatomical assessment of the posterior deltoid as a potentially safer injection target. Key ResultsO_LIThe deltoid muscles of 5,239 participants from the UK Biobank matching UK annual influenza vaccination eligibility were segmented using a deep learning-based model, enabling precise volumetric quantification of the anterior, middle and posterior deltoids. C_LIO_LIThe posterior deltoid demonstrated a larger average muscle volume when compared to the middle volume across vaccine-eligible groups and sexes (p<0.0001). C_LIO_LIThese findings provide a comprehensive reference framework for deltoid assessment across different ages and genders, enhancing both research and clinical decision-making for IM injection site selection. C_LI Summary statementAutomated deltoid volumetry in a pilot UK Biobank cohort revealed greater posterior than middle deltoid volume, supporting further evaluation of the posterior deltoid for a potential alternative intramuscular vaccination site.

title: Silent Drift and Site-level Variance in Clinical AI: Real-world performance and subgroup analysis for post-market monitoring of an FDA-cleared artificial intelligence (AI) triage tool for high-risk use case of pulmonary embolism
abstract: BackgroundFDA-cleared artificial intelligence (AI) triage tool for pulmonary embolism (PE) detection has been widely used; however, its performance has not been analyzed for subgroups, clinical sites, and temporal stability. MethodsThis retrospective, six-site health system study evaluated the Aidoc BriefCase PE triage model (K190072) across 14,736 CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) examinations between July 2023 and March 2026. Reference-standard PE characteristic labels were extracted from radiology reports using a zero-shot LLM pipeline validated against a radiologist-annotated 600 reports ({kappa} =0.98). Model performance was evaluated across demographics, embolus characteristics, and site. Temporal behavior was evaluated on operating point by logistic regression, with and without site adjustment, and by segmented regression. ResultsPE was present in 1,402/14,736 examinations (9.5%). Overall sensitivity was 64.1% (95% CI, 61.5-66.6%), specificity 98.8% (95% CI, 98.6-99.0%), compared with 93% sensitivity and 93.7% specificity in the FDA 510(k) summary. Sensitivity fell with peripherality (central 88.6%, lobar or segmental 63.1%, subsegmental 33.3%) and with chronicity (acute 65.5%, chronic 57.4%). Sensitivity differed significantly between the two highest-volume sites, 68.7% and 55.7% (P < .001), with CT scanner as the only variable different between the two sites. The false-positive rate fell 40% per year (P<.001) at a similar rate at two sites, while sensitivity fell 15% per year at site A (P<.036), from 72.5% to 65.0% between two halves of the study period. The manufacturer did not report model updates or threshold changes during the study period. ConclusionsDeployed sensitivity was substantially below the cleared benchmark and varied 13 points by site. The gradual shift in high specificity at the cost of low sensitivity, either from data drift or threshold change, either not monitored or not documented by the manufacturer, highlights the importance of independent continuous post-market monitoring.

BackgroundFDA-cleared artificial intelligence (AI) triage tool for pulmonary embolism (PE) detection has been widely used; however, its performance has not been analyzed for subgroups, clinical sites, and temporal stability.

MethodsThis retrospective, six-site health system study evaluated the Aidoc BriefCase PE triage model (K190072) across 14,736 CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) examinations between July 2023 and March 2026. Reference-standard PE characteristic labels were extracted from radiology reports using a zero-shot LLM pipeline validated against a radiologist-annotated 600 reports ({kappa} =0.98). Model performance was evaluated across demographics, embolus characteristics, and site. Temporal behavior was evaluated on operating point by logistic regression, with and without site adjustment, and by segmented regression.

ResultsPE was present in 1,402/14,736 examinations (9.5%). Overall sensitivity was 64.1% (95% CI, 61.5-66.6%), specificity 98.8% (95% CI, 98.6-99.0%), compared with 93% sensitivity and 93.7% specificity in the FDA 510(k) summary. Sensitivity fell with peripherality (central 88.6%, lobar or segmental 63.1%, subsegmental 33.3%) and with chronicity (acute 65.5%, chronic 57.4%). Sensitivity differed significantly between the two highest-volume sites, 68.7% and 55.7% (P < .001), with CT scanner as the only variable different between the two sites. The false-positive rate fell 40% per year (P<.001) at a similar rate at two sites, while sensitivity fell 15% per year at site A (P<.036), from 72.5% to 65.0% between two halves of the study period. The manufacturer did not report model updates or threshold changes during the study period.

ConclusionsDeployed sensitivity was substantially below the cleared benchmark and varied 13 points by site. The gradual shift in high specificity at the cost of low sensitivity, either from data drift or threshold change, either not monitored or not documented by the manufacturer, highlights the importance of independent continuous post-market monitoring.

title: Deep Learning Identifies BMI-Associated Morphologic Features in Breast Cancer Tissue
abstract: A bstract Multiple epidemiological studies have established obesity as an adverse factor in breast cancer incidence, progression, and clinical outcomes. However, the biological mechanisms underlying these associations remain incompletely understood. In peritumoral adipose tissue, obesity is associated with chronic inflammation, macrophage recruitment, and broader alterations in the local microenvironment. Whether these obesity-associated changes are accompanied by distinct morphologic features within the tumor and non-adipose stromal compartments remains unclear. In this study, we investigated whether an AI-based pathology foundation model could support the development of machine learning algorithms capable of identifying obesity-associated morphologic patterns in histopathology images, with a particular focus on tumor and stromal regions. In a cohort of 195 patients with breast cancer, machine learning models using vector embeddings from non-adipose stromal regions classified high BMI (≥30 kg/m 2 ) versus low BMI (<25 kg/m 2 ) with an average AUC of 0.78 (95% CI: 0.73–0.83), consistently outperforming models based on tumor-only or combined tumor–stroma regions. These obesity-associated stromal signatures were observed across subgroups defined by hormone-receptor status and age, indicating that they are not restricted to specific clinical populations. Complementary embedding-based dissimilarity analysis further showed that higher BMI was associated with reduced inter-patient heterogeneity in both tumor and stromal tissues. Overall, these findings suggest that obesity is associated with distinct morphologic alterations in both tumor and non-adipose stromal tissues. Notably, the stromal compartment emerged as a particularly informative indicator of obesity-associated morphology and demonstrated reduced inter-patient heterogeneity among individuals with high BMI.

title: Understanding robustness and enabling remediation of neuroimaging-based deep neural networks for digital security: Semantic segmentation of brain tumors as illustrative study
abstract: Abstract Background: Applications of deep learning models in neuroimaging have significantly advanced translational neuroscience, offering substantial benefits to human health. However, recent cybersecurity threats have undermined the reliability of digital neuroscience tools, posing challenges to the clinical neuroscience community. A critical issue is the automated semantic segmentation of malignant or premalignant brain tumors, essential for neurosurgery and radiotherapy planning. New methods: This study investigates the robustness of customary deep learning models such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and more recent Vision Transformers (ViTs) in semantic segmentation against adversarial attacks. We assess the performance of CNNs and ViTs under ideal nonhostile conditions and then under cybersecurity threats. Results: Our findings reveal that while CNNs perform well in ideal conditions, their efficiency sharply declines under adversarial perturbations. In contrast, ViTs maintain their segmentation performance even when subjected to adversarial attacks. This study is the first to apply Visual Transformers for cybersecurity challenge, leveraging advanced capabilities of VITs to enhance robustness against digital perturbations. Comparison with existing methods: Compared to CNNs, which are widely used for neuroimages but vulnerable to adversarial attacks, ViTs demonstrate superior resilience. Our research highlights that ViTs are as effective as CNNs under ideal conditions but offer enhanced protection from cybersecurity angle, making them a more robust choice for neuroimaging applications. Conclusion: Our results indicate that for large-scale segmentation operation in neuroimaging, such as lesion segmentation tasks, ViT-based models should be preferred over CNN-based models. This shift could provide inherent protection against prevalent digital threats, ensuring more reliable and secure neuroimaging diagnostics.

title: A Multi-Cohort nnU-Net for White Matter Hyperintensity Segmentation Across 2D and 3D FLAIR Acquisitions
abstract: ABSTRACT Background White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are increasingly pooled across aging, cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD), and dementia cohorts that differ in both disease composition and FLAIR acquisition. Most automated segmentation tools were developed within a narrower range of populations or protocols, and few have been tested for whether segmentation accuracy and error remain consistent across conventional 2D and isotropic 3D FLAIR, or whether the choice of algorithm alters downstream clinical associations. Methods We developed a single nnU-Net model, taking FLAIR and T1-weighted images as inputs, using 460 2D and 3D FLAIR scans from a neurodegenerative cohort (Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, ADNI), a CSVD-enriched cohort with same-visit paired 2D and 3D FLAIR (Washington University White Matter Ischemic-Hypoxia study, WWISH), and a population-based sample (UK Biobank), holding out 92 scans from 66 participants at the participant-level as an internal test set. We further evaluated the model in an independent ADNI3 3D FLAIR set (n = 25), benchmarking voxel-wise overlap (Dice), volumetric agreement, and lesion-level detection against SHIVA-WMH, segcsvdWMH, and FreeSurfer WMH-SynthSeg, and compared acquisition-specific volume bias in participants with paired 2D and 3D FLAIR. We then compared how WMH volumes from each method predicted incident dementia in cognitively unimpaired adults from ADNI and the Knight Alzheimer Disease Research Center (n = 1,174; 42 incident cases). Results In the internal test set, the model achieved a mean Dice of 0.73 (SD 0.10), compared with 0.50, 0.57, and 0.29 for SHIVA-WMH, segcsvdWMH, and WMH-SynthSeg (all FDR-adjusted p < 0.001). Dice was similar on 2D and 3D FLAIR (0.75 vs. 0.71). In WWISH participants imaged with both acquisitions, mean volume bias differed between 2D and 3D scans by 1.8 mL for the model versus 4.7–9.9 mL for the comparators. Advantages were largest in low-burden scans (<5 mL; Dice 0.66 vs. 0.19–0.54) and for lesions of ≤100 voxels (detection 77–87% vs. 14–63%). In ADNI3, the model retained a mean Dice of 0.70 (SD 0.14) without retraining and exceeded all comparators (FDR-adjusted p ≤ 0.002). Model-derived WMH volume was associated with incident dementia beyond clinical covariates (OR per SD 1.40, 95% CI 1.11–1.77; likelihood-ratio p = 0.009; cross-validated AUC 0.71 vs. 0.68), whereas comparator-derived volumes did not significantly improve model fit. Conclusions Training a single model across disease contexts and FLAIR acquisitions yielded WMH segmentation that was similarly accurate on 2D and 3D FLAIR, sensitive to low-burden disease, transferable to an unseen protocol, and clinically informative, supporting its use in multi-cohort, mixed-etiology studies. KEY POINTS A single nnU-Net trained across neurodegenerative, cerebral small vessel disease, and population-based cohorts and across 2D and 3D FLAIR outperformed SHIVA-WMH, segcsvdWMH, and WMH-SynthSeg, with the largest gains in low-burden scans and small lesions. In same-visit paired 2D and 3D FLAIR scans, the model’s volume bias relative to acquisition-specific reference masks varied less across acquisitions, whereas comparator biases varied with acquisition. Only WMH volume from the model significantly improved model fit for incident dementia beyond clinical covariates, highlighting the potential influence of segmentation algorithm choice on downstream clinical inference.

title: Reliability-Aware Clinical Relation Learning for Uncertainty-Robust Multi-Label Chest X-ray Classification
abstract: Background Automated multi-label classification of chest radiographs is complicated by overlapping imaging findings, noisy report-derived labels, and changes in disease co-occurrence across clinical settings. Existing clinical-hierarchy methods can encode label relationships, but a rigid hierarchy may conflate categorical membership with empirical association and propagate annotation errors. Methods We investigated Reliability-Aware Clinical Relation Learning (ReCaRL), a graph-assisted framework for multi-label chest radiograph classification. An image encoder produces initial finding scores, while a graph constructed from training-label associations provides reliability-weighted, confidence-gated updates. Uncertain annotations are handled with observation masks. The evaluation compares flat, weighted, graph-based, and hierarchy-penalty baselines, with internal and external discrimination and calibration assessments. Results In the internal evaluation, ReCaRL achieved macro AUROC 0.821 and macro AUPRC 0.437, compared with 0.812 and 0.423 for the masked/weighted baseline. Mean AUROC across five common findings was 0.865 versus 0.858. External testing yielded AUROC 0.799 and AUPRC 0.409. Post-hoc calibration reduced the internal Brier score from 0.113 to 0.102 and the external expected calibration error from 0.082 to 0.061, without changing AUROC or AUPRC. Conclusions Reliability-aware graph propagation and confidence gating were associated with modest improvements in multi-label chest radiograph classification relative to the matched masked/weighted baseline. Post-hoc calibration improved probability reliability in the reported evaluations. The findings do not establish a benefit in prospective clinical decision-making.
