title: Within-scan MRI signal and texture in Alzheimer disease: a multicohort study
abstract: INTRODUCTIONConventional MRI contains tissue signal and texture information beyond regional volume, but acquisition variability limits their comparability. We evaluated within-scan signal and texture analyses for estimating contemporaneous cognition and amyloid/tau burden in Alzheimers disease (AD) beyond volumetry. METHODSWe retrospectively analyzed 2,437 baseline datasets from ADNI3, ADNI4, MCSA, SCAN/CLARiTI, and OASIS-3. SynthSeg defined regions for T1-weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) measurements. Within-scan regional-to-rest log ratios (WSRLR) were compared with scanner-matched, cross-fitted cognitively normal (CN) references. Texture analysis used three-dimensional gray-level co-occurrence matrices (GLCM). Covariate-adjusted rank models examined associations; ADNI3-trained ridge, elastic-net, gradient-boosting, and TabPFN-v2 models were tested externally. RESULTSModerate-to-strong correlations were observed between regional signal changes assessed using WSRLR vs. CN-reference (cohort median regional {rho}=0.504-0.890; n=2,314). Lower entorhinal FLAIR WSRLR and greater entropy were associated with AD dementia adjusted for volume, while opposite correlations were observed with the hippocampus (all q<0.001). Greater entorhinal FLAIR entropy correlated with lower Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) scores (r=-0.198 and -0.098, respectively; both q<0.001). Lower entorhinal FLAIR WSRLR and T1 cluster shade were associated with higher regional tau uptake beyond volume and diagnosis (r=-0.146 and -0.205; both q[≤]0.010). Adding entorhinal and hippocampal signal and texture significantly improved pooled external MoCA (n=868) and MMSE (n=551) prediction in three of four models. DISCUSSIONWithin-scan signal and texture demonstrated AD-related regional associations and improved prediction of contemporaneous cognitive performance beyond volumetry. Prospective validation is needed to evaluate their potential value in opportunistic dementia screening.

title: Adapting Echocardiographic Foundation Models for Detecting Pulmonary Embolism-Related Right-Heart Strain
abstract: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a time-sensitive medical emergency in which rapid recognition of right ventricular (RV) dysfunction by point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) can support early risk stratification. Here, we present HOPE (ecHO-Pulmonary Embolism), a real-world emergency cardiac POCUS video dataset comprising 4,069 patients with suspected PE, and EchoPE1, a foundation-model-based video classification framework for detecting PE-associated right-heart phenotypes. HOPE includes five commonly acquired emergency echocardiographic views, with all positive PE cases confirmed by computed tomography pulmonary angiography. EchoPE builds on EchoPrime-pretrained echocardiographic representations and incorporates view recognition, task-specific adaptation, and attention-based interpretability. Experiments suggested that directly transferring EchoPrime representations to this disease-specific task provided limited performance, whereas EchoPE (AUROC 95.2 {+/-} .3) substantially outperformed both EchoPrime with a classification head (AUROC 87.6 {+/-} 1) and conventional video deep learning baselines. At a fixed sensitivity of 90%, EchoPE achieved a precision of 87.8, compared with 70.7 for EchoPrime. Among adaptation strategies, Low-Rank Adaptation combined with knowledge distillation provided the best balance between PE discrimination and preservation of pretrained echocardiographic semantics. Interpretability analyses showed that the adapted model focused on clinically relevant RV morphological changes, interventricular septal configuration, and informative temporal segments within ultrasound videos. Overall, HOPE and EchoPE demonstrate that echocardiographic foundation models require dataset-specific adaptation to identify PE-related right-heart strain and support the potential use of artificial intelligence-assisted bedside echocardiography for risk warning in acute care settings.

title: EpiCycle: A flexible approach for scalable, three-dimensional reconstructions of complex epithelial tissues
abstract: Understanding organ development and repair requires methods to precisely describe cell geometry. Recent image analysis methods allow increasingly accurate segmentation of simple epithelial tissues. However, many vertebrate organs contain more complex stratified epithelia, for which accurate 3D cellular segmentation remains challenging. Here, we describe EpiCycle, an iterative, user-friendly approach developed to address the unique segmentation challenges posed by stratified epithelia. Starting from sparse or no ground truth annotations, EpiCycle guides users through a human-in-the-loop refinement process that culminates in 3D consensus reconstruction. Through cyclical correction, annotation and model retraining, EpiCycle allows users to progressively build robust, dataset-specific segmentation models while simultaneously generating 3D ground truth. To highlight the utility of EpiCycle, we train models that generate high-confidence, tissue-level segmentation of the stratified squamous epithelium in adult zebrafish skin. We apply our approach to segmentation of mouse embryonic branching salivary glands demonstrating its versatility across organs and species. Finally, we produce and analyze quantitative measurements of stratified cell geometry in human fetal epidermis. Thus, EpiCycle enables scalable and quantitative 3D reconstructions of complex vertebrate tissues without relying on pre-existing ground truth.

title: Being Born versus Being Born Early: Disentangling Birth from Prematurity in Perinatal Brain Development
abstract: ABSTRACT Studies of preterm birth report both delayed and accelerated brain maturation, depending on whether preterm infants are compared with term newborns or with fetuses. We propose that these mixed observations arise because such comparisons conflate two distinct influences, the effect of birth on term-aged infants and the independent effects of being born prematurely. Using MRI data from 330 term and 118 preterm neonates in the developing Human Connectome Project (dHCP), we developed a simple piecewise linear model that estimates prenatal and postnatal rates of development separately for term and preterm infants across volumetric, microstructural and connectivity measures. In term infants, birth accelerated volumetric growth, with total brain volume growing 44% faster post-birth, with regionally specific alterations in microstructural trajectories. Deep white matter continued to mature, whereas superficial and cerebellar white matter reversed direction. Changes in cortical connectivity at birth followed the sensorimotor to association axis, shifting towards specialisation in sensory and insular cortex and towards more diverse connectivity in association cortex. In contrast, the effect of birth on preterm infants was much weaker, where development largely continued at prenatal rates. These results show that the impact of birth depends on brain region and maturational state at birth. Separating birth from prematurity offers a framework for interpreting mixed findings in the perinatal literature.

Studies of preterm birth report both delayed and accelerated brain maturation, depending on whether preterm infants are compared with term newborns or with fetuses. We propose that these mixed observations arise because such comparisons conflate two distinct influences, the effect of birth on term-aged infants and the independent effects of being born prematurely. Using MRI data from 330 term and 118 preterm neonates in the developing Human Connectome Project (dHCP), we developed a simple piecewise linear model that estimates prenatal and postnatal rates of development separately for term and preterm infants across volumetric, microstructural and connectivity measures. In term infants, birth accelerated volumetric growth, with total brain volume growing 44% faster post-birth, with regionally specific alterations in microstructural trajectories. Deep white matter continued to mature, whereas superficial and cerebellar white matter reversed direction. Changes in cortical connectivity at birth followed the sensorimotor to association axis, shifting towards specialisation in sensory and insular cortex and towards more diverse connectivity in association cortex. In contrast, the effect of birth on preterm infants was much weaker, where development largely continued at prenatal rates. These results show that the impact of birth depends on brain region and maturational state at birth. Separating birth from prematurity offers a framework for interpreting mixed findings in the perinatal literature.

title: Confidence-Aware Adaptation for Medical Image Segmentation Under Acquisition Shift
abstract: Medical image segmentation models can lose accuracy and produce unreliable confidence estimates when deployed across acquisition centres. We study StaRFM, an adaptation objective that combines a Fisher information penalty (FIP) with a confidence misalignment penalty (CMP), and examine how the spatial aggregation of CMP affects lesion segmentation. We evaluate a Segment Anything Model (SAM) adaptation on five MRI and CT datasets and conduct a controlled leave-centre-out experiment on ISLES~2022 using a 3D U-Net. The SAM experiments improve mean Dice by 2.3 percentage points relative to fine-tuned SAM; calibration was not measured for those models. In the ISLES experiment, the baseline achieved 73.0\% Dice, 7.71\% boundary expected calibration error (bECE), and $1.03\times10^{-2}$ negative log-likelihood (NLL) on 52 held-out-centre cases. A class-balanced CMP variant achieved 74.8\% Dice, 6.57\% bECE, and $0.59\times10^{-2}$ NLL; a boundary-restricted variant achieved 74.1\% Dice, 6.24\% bECE, and $0.58\times10^{-2}$ NLL. In contrast, stronger voxel-averaged CMP reduced Dice, and FIP offered no measurable additional benefit in this controlled study. Because the balanced and boundary variants were developed after an initial negative experiment, these results are exploratory. Complementary vision-language experiments and mathematical analysis characterise the broader objective, without establishing clinical reliability or a general calibration guarantee under shift. Our findings highlight the importance of class imbalance and boundary-aware evaluation when designing confidence penalties for medical segmentation.

title: Disentangling within-cell-type heterogeneity from transcript contamination in imaging-based spatial transcriptomics
abstract: Recent advances in imaging-based spatial transcriptomics have enabled high-resolution characterization of gene expression and cellular organization in situ. Resolving within-cell-type heterogeneity is essential for understanding how cellular states relate to tissue function and disease. However, imperfect cell segmentation and RNA spillover can contaminate cell-level expression profiles, obscuring intrinsic expression patterns and generating spurious variation. Existing decontamination methods can struggle to distinguish intrinsic variation from contamination when both are inferred from spatial measurements alone, and may suppress genuine state-associated signals when within-cell-type heterogeneity is not explicitly modeled. Here we present Dancer, a reference-guided probabilistic framework that disentangles within-cell-type heterogeneity from transcript contamination by combining cell-type-specific gene programs learned from single-cell data with explicit modeling of intrinsic expression, neighboring-cell contamination and background RNA. Across multiple human tumor datasets with varying gene compositions and panel sizes, Dancer improves cell-type separation and expression specificity while preserving identity-associated signals, achieving superior overall performance in benchmark comparisons. Inferred gene program activities reveal within-cell-type heterogeneity in the form of distinct cellular states and continuous spatial gradients associated with local tissue environments, while reference-guided panel expansion extends molecular characterization beyond the measured genes. Together, Dancer supports accurate transcript decontamination and more faithful interpretation of cellular heterogeneity within its native tissue context.

title: Centiloid Calibration and Application of MUSE-Based Amyloid PET Quantification for Florbetapir (AV-45)
abstract: Introduction Amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) quantifies cerebral {beta}-amyloid in Alzheimer's disease (AD), but tracer- and processing-dependent variability limits comparability. We evaluated Centiloid transformations for multi-atlas segmentation (MUSE)-based [11C]Pittsburgh compound B (PiB) and [18F]florbetapir (AV-45) PET. Methods Standardized uptake value ratio (SUVr) Centiloid transformations without partial-volume correction (NoPVC) and with parallel level set regularization-based PVC (PLS-PVC) were calibrated using the original Klunk Centiloid PiB reference dataset (N = 79) and paired PiB-AV-45 Navitsky dataset (N = 43). Centiloid transformations were evaluated in Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI; AV-45) and secondarily in Knight Alzheimer Disease Research Center (Knight-ADRC; PiB) cohorts. Outcomes included AD-cognitively normal (CN) separation and clinical associations. Scanner effects were examined in ADNI. Results MUSE-derived PiB SUVr measurements corresponded strongly with reference measurements (R2 = 0.963, ICC(A,1) = 0.981), and PiB-AV-45 cross-tracer correspondence was high (R2 = 0.873-0.884). NoPVC separated AD from CN in Knight-ADRC PiB (Hedges' g = 1.907) and ADNI AV-45 (g = 0.892). PLS-PVC yielded similar separation in Knight-ADRC ({Delta}g = -0.027; 95% CI -0.122 to 0.023) and modestly greater separation in ADNI ({Delta}g = 0.053; 95% CI 0.038-0.068). Scanner-associated variance represented 33.5% of total Centiloid variance in ADNI; on scanners other than one older model, AD-CN separation was larger (g = 1.31). Both approaches showed clinical associations. Discussion MUSE Centiloid transformations provide a framework for expressing PiB and AV-45 measurements in Centiloid units across independent cohorts. Scanner and processing differences warrant scanner-specific quality checks and cautious interpretation.

title: Automated CTA-Based Assessment of Aortic Remodeling Through Volumetric Biomarkers in Type B Aortic Dissection
abstract: Type B aortic dissection (TBAD) requires lifelong morphological monitoring using computed tomography angiography (CTA). TBAD separates blood flow into the true lumen (TL), the original aortic channel, and the false lumen (FL), created by the dissection. Although three-dimensional volumetric analysis may complement diameter-based surveillance, its clinical adoption is limited by the time required for manual segmentation, particularly in postoperative scans affected by metallic artifacts. This study developed and evaluated an automated CTA-based framework for volumetric surveillance of TBAD across native and post-TEVAR conditions. We propose AORTA-SCAN, a hierarchical multi-stage framework for automated segmentation of the aorta, TL, and FL, extended to stented anatomy through a metal-aware triple-input strategy. The system computes conventional diameter measurements and volumetric biomarkers, including the perfusion dissection index (PDI), defined as the ratio between perfused FL volume and total perfused aortic volume. Domain adaptation was achieved using transfer learning and partial-label learning across heterogeneous clinical annotations. In native cases, AORTA-SCAN achieved a global Dice score of 0.84 and significantly improved FL segmentation compared with the nnU-Net baseline (0.84 vs 0.71, p < 0.001). Volumetric analysis showed high agreement with expert references, with a mean PDI bias of -0.17%. In postoperative cases, TL segmentation remained robust (Dice = 0.90), while FL and stent Dice were 0.75 and 0.72, respectively. Processing was completed in less than 1 minute per case on a standard workstation. AORTA-SCAN enables automated volumetric surveillance of TBAD and supports scalable extraction of PDI and diameter biomarkers from native and post-TEVAR CTA.

title: Integrating Plasma Brain-Derived pTau217, White Matter Hyperintensity and Hippocampal Volumes as Optimized Prognostic Markers for Cognitive Decline in an Asian Cohort with High Cerebrovascular Disease Burden
abstract: Abstract Background: Combination of plasma and neuroimaging biomarkers associated with Alzheimer's disease (AD) and cerebrovascular pathophysiology might provide more accurate prediction of cognitive decline in populations with extensive AD and cerebral small vessel disease copathologies. Here, we aimed to identify an optimized biomarker panel for predicting cognitive decline by evaluating combinations of plasma and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) biomarkers. Methods: We investigated participants without dementia or with mild dementia, recruited from memory clinics and the community in Singapore between August 2010 and August 2020. Plasma biomarkers of brain amyloid (brain-derived [BD]-pTau217, BD-pTau181, BD-pTau231, total-pTau217, total-pTau181, and total-pTau231), astrogliosis (GFAP), and neuroaxonal injury (NfL), with MRI measures of cerebrovascular disease (white matter hyperintensity [WMH] volume) and neurodegeneration (hippocampal volume), and primary outcome of longitudinal Clinical Dementia Rating Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB; mean [SD] follow-up duration, 51.0 [15.8] months). All plasma and MRI biomarker combinations for predicting CDR-SB slope (annual change in CDR-SB) were evaluated. Results: This study included 523 participants (mean [SD] age, 72.4 [7.9] years; 291 females [55.6%]). The parsimonious model included plasma BD-pTau217, WMH volume, and hippocampal volume (all P ≤ 0.004). Dichotomizing these biomarkers yielded A, V, and N status, respectively, classifying participants as all negative (A-V-N-; n = 128), 1-positive (A+V-N-, A-V+N- or A-V-N+; n = 154), 2-positive (A+V+N-, A+V-N+, A-V+N+;n = 158) or 3-positive (A+V+N+; n = 83). Annual CDR-SB progression increased stepwise with the number of positive biomarkers. Compared with the all negative group (β, 0.016), the 1-positive (β, 0.409), 2-positive (β, 1.16) and 3-positive groups (β, 1.49) showed faster cognitive decline (all P < 0.001). Moreover, the 2-positive and 3-positive groups progressed faster than the 1-positive group (both P < 0.001), and the 3-positive group declined faster than 2-positive group (P = 0.009). Conclusions: Presence of multiple pathophysiological processes was associated with greater cognitive decline, highlighting the utility of a comprehensive multimodal biomarker profile to enhance prognostication.

title: Mucinous Pancreatic Cysts: A Single-Center Experience Epidemiology, Surveillance, Risk Formulation, Surgery
abstract: Background: Mucinous pancreatic cysts demonstrate malignant risk and expanding prevalence. Society guidelines lack underpinning from large, single-center experiences. We describe pancreatic mucinous cyst epidemiology, compare cyst-derived cancers from surveilled vs. non-surveilled cohorts, analyze risk metrics using surveillance and pathologic outcomes, and propose a weighted cancer risk probability score. Methods We conducted a retrospective study of patients at a tertiary metropolitan hospital between January 2006 and December 2025 who were found to have a mucinous pancreatic cyst or cyst-derived cancer on endoscopic ultrasound (EUS). A diagnostic algorithm was used to presumptively diagnose cyst phenotypes; diagnoses were clarified through surveillance and surgery. A preliminary risk classification scheme categorized patients to a risk level based on six binary variables. Cyst-derived cancer (CDCa) were categorized by first encounter or progression from surveillance. Survival analysis of surgical patients was organized by histologic grade and tumor stage. We developed a new malignant progression risk formula that weighted the four most predictive risk metrics: cyst size, main duct phenotype, pancreatic duct dilation, and bile duct dilation. Results 3667 cysts in 3643 patients were analyzed; 2087 (57%) were branch duct and 93 (2.9%) were main duct intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMN), and 79 (2.4%) were mucinous cystic neoplasms (MCN). Unclassifiable cysts (n = 1386, 32%) were analyzed as a primordial branch duct IPMN cohort due to volume and gender equivalents. IPMN-MD were often mislabeled as IPMN-BD during surveillance (43%). Our initial recommended surveillance interval was based on six unweighted metrics: solid nodule, pancreatic or bile duct dilation, main duct involvement, and fluid chemistry. Cyst-derived cancers developed in 8% of mucinous cysts (n = 162). Resection was performed in 184 patients from surveilled (n = 76) and non-surveilled (n = 108) cohorts. Surveilled patients had fewer advanced stage cancers; however, explant pathology was low/moderate dysplasia in 72 resected patients. Kaplan-Meier survival at 5 years was 82% with high-grade dysplasia and T1N0 and 50% for T2N0 and T3N0 lesions. Frequencies of malignant cyst progression were main duct IPMNs (53%), branch duct IPMN (6%), and MCN (5%). Mucinous cyst-derived cancers accounted for 10.7% of all pancreatic adenocarcinomas within our registry. Our logistic regression model achieved a cross-validated area under the ROC of 0.957 (95% CI: 0.944–0.968), with 90% sensitivity at a threshold corresponding to 90% specificity. Conclusion In this longitudinal cohort study, branch duct IPMN was the dominant phenotype, yet main duct IPMN was most likely to progress to malignancy. Surveillance favored early cancer diagnosis yet with low specificity. Post resection survival was excellent and explant pathology revealed lower frequency of nodal disease when compared to PDAC. Risk metric analysis led to a new risk-formulation strategy for patient selection. Our new weighted risk formula offers high predictive accuracy, helping to avoid unnecessary resections.

title: A test-retest reliability and multiverse analysis of denoising pipelines in four common functional MRI task paradigms
abstract: Test–retest reliability is a key issue in functional MRI research, yet it is unclear how reliability differs across commonly used task paradigms, and the effect denoising pipelines may have on reliability measures. The present study used four tasks designed to probe a range of cognitive/emotional domains: N–back (working memory), Go/No–Go (response inhibition), Monetary Incentive Delay (MID; reward processing), and OASIS (emotional images) task. Healthy participants (N=25) completed all four tasks in two scanning sessions. Analyses used fMRIPrep for spatial preprocessing. Twelve subsequent denoising pipelines were then implemented, combining head–motion parameters (6 vs. 24), tissue–based regressors, 'aCompCor' components and head–motion spike regressors. An additional 'multiverse' analysis produced a consensus result across these pipelines. The performance of each pipeline in driving robust statistical results was assessed using residual motion–related variance, mean Z statistics, and the number of suprathreshold (Z=3.1, p<0.05, cluster–corrected) voxels. Reliability across sessions was quantified using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC(3,1)), Dice coefficients, and Spearman's correlations. Denoising pipeline had limited effects on mean Z statistics, but strongly influenced the spatial extent of suprathreshold clusters, particularly on the event–related tasks (Go/No–Go and MID). No single denoising pipeline was shown to be optimal across all tasks, and pipeline effects were present for different contrasts within the same (emotional pictures) task. Inclusion of motion spike regressors did not confer any benefits compared to similar pipelines without spike regressors. The N–back task was the most reliable (ICC: ~0.45, Dice: ~0.8, Spearman's: >0.9) while the Go/No–Go was the least reliable (ICC: ~0.1, Dice: ~0.3, Spearman's: ~0.6). Group–level reliability measures (Dice, Spearman's) showed higher values than the individual–level measure (ICC). Tasks producing the strongest activation levels (N–back, emotional images) showed the highest reliability and the least sensitivity to differences in denoising approach. This suggests that task selection, experimental design, and overall experimental power are likely to be more critical determinants of reliability than analytic decisions.

title: Interrater Reliability of Clinical Resting-State fMRI Network Classification: Comparison of Human Raters and an AI Algorithm
abstract: PurposeAccurate classification of intrinsic brain networks is essential for the clinical interpretation of resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI), especially in complex pediatric populations. Manual classification of resting-state networks (RSNs) remains the clinical gold standard, yet variability among raters poses a challenge for reproducibility. This study aims to assess interrater reliability among five human raters and one AI algorithm. MethodsRs-fMRI data were collected from 269 scans in a clinical cohort predominantly composed of pediatric patients. Raters used an independent component analysis (ICA)-based pipeline to categorize RSNs into one of 13 categories. Percent agreement, Cohens Kappa, and Fleisss Kappa were used to measure agreement. ResultsOverall pairwise agreement for human-human pairs ranged from substantial to almost perfect ({kappa} = 0.655-0.845), while human-AI agreement ranged from fair to moderate ({kappa} = 0.289-0.401). Agreement was highest for Typical networks and Noise, whereas Atypical networks showed lower agreement, with moderate human-human agreement ({kappa} = 0.468-0.541) and poor-to-fair human-AI agreement ({kappa} = 0.147-0.305). Despite high human-human agreement on Noise components, human-AI kappa values for Noise were disproportionately low, a pattern that may reflect the high prevalence of Noise components and class imbalance in the models training data. ConclusionOur findings underscore the need for standardized classification frameworks and targeted training to improve consistency, particularly for atypical networks. This study supports the development of reproducible rs-fMRI workflows and the potential use of AI as a complementary screening tool within clinical neuroimaging workflows.

title: A coordinate-to-coordinate machine learning framework for contrast-agnostic brain target localization
abstract: Representing a structure by a coordinate can be challenging particularly for structures which lack conspicuity, whether due to their small size, lack of contrast, or image artifact. In this paper, we developed a machine learning framework to localize brain targets from the coordinates of salient brain landmarks (i.e., coordinate-to-coordinate) that is agnostic to image contrast. We make use of a validated brain landmark annotation protocol inspired by classical stereotactic methods and a dataset which spans a wide range of MRI field strengths and neurodegenerative diseases. We apply this framework to predict deep brain stimulation targets, achieving an accuracy of 1-1.5 mm validated against expert rater annotations on ultra-high field (UHF) MRI. Results demonstrated comparable localization accuracy on test-retest data acquired using both standard and UHF MRI. Our proposed framework outperformed deformable registration on clinical MRI and performed comparably on multispectral UHF MRI. We deployed our model in the form of a website (stereotaxy.afids.io) and openly release all coordinate data. This framework is agnostic to MRI contrast and offers a method for rapid coordinate localization with applications more broadly in neuroimaging as well as for specialized settings like surgical planning.

title: Synthetic Magnetic Resonance Spectra Generation using convex NMF in Neuro-Oncology
abstract: Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy is a powerful, non-invasive technique for investigating the metabolic composition of biological tissues, particularly useful in the classification of brain tumours. However, its inclusion into machine learning pipelines is limited by the scarcity of large, labelled datasets. This work evaluates whether synthetic MR spectra generated using convex Non-negative Matrix Factorisation and probabilistic modelling of the resulting weight distributions can improve brain tumour classification. MR spectra from the INTERPRET database were decomposed into interpretable source and weight matrices, both separately for each of six diagnostic tasks and jointly across five tissue classes, at short and long echo time. Class-specific weight distributions were modelled using Gaussian Mixture Models and Kernel Density Estimation across a range of hyperparameter settings, and new weight vectors were sampled and recombined with the fixed source matrix to produce synthetic spectra; hyperparameters were selected by the mean squared error to the real class means. The diagnostic utility of the synthetic spectra was assessed with Linear Discriminant Analysis under three internal and four external evaluation strategies, the latter using an independent multi-centre cohort. Synthetic spectra were readily classified by models trained on real data (mean accuracy 0.87), but models trained on synthetic spectra alone generalised poorly, both to real INTERPRET spectra (0.55) and to the external cohort (0.47, against 0.84 for training on real data; p [≤] 0.003). Augmenting real training data with synthetic spectra neither improved nor significantly harmed external accuracy (mean paired differences between -0.04 and +0.01; all p [≥] 0.027 uncorrected, none significant after correction), and class-balanced augmentation did not help, and task-specific and joint decompositions performed comparably. The selected generative models were low in complexity and produced spectra closer to the class means than the real data are, suggesting that selection by reconstruction fidelity is poorly aligned with the goal of augmentation, and that internal validation alone would have overstated the value of the synthetic data.

title: SYNDRI: Context-aware removal of transcript spillover in imaging-based spatial transcriptomics
abstract: Imaging-based spatial transcriptomics (ST) measures gene expression at single-cell resolution, but imperfect segmentation often misassigns transcripts between neighboring cells, a problem known as transcript spillover. This spillover is niche-dependent and can therefore confound downstream analyses that rely on niche-specific differential expression. True spillover cannot be directly quantified in experimental ST data, so existing correction methods infer contamination indirectly from transcript positions or expression structure. Here we introduce SYNDRI, a post-segmentation correction method that frames spillover detection as a supervised, gene-level classification task. We develop SYNDRI-SIM to generate labeled training data by simulating spillover between spatially mapped scRNA-seq profiles. SYNDRI uses a transformer to predict gene-level spillover probabilities conditioned on each cell's expression, identity, and local neighborhood, without requiring transcript-level coordinates or deconvolution. On held-out simulated data, SYNDRI achieves an AUPRC of 0.86, compared with 0.64 for the next-best method. Across MERFISH, CosMx, and Xenium datasets, SYNDRI achieves the highest aggregate performance across metrics of cell-type separation, reference similarity, and preservation of within-cell-type heterogeneity. In a CosMx lung cancer dataset, SYNDRI removes nearly all potentially contaminating tumor and macrophage markers from differential expression between tumor-associated and stromal fibroblasts while retaining native fibroblast markers. These results demonstrate the utility of learning from simulated spillover to improve the interpretation of spatial gene expression.
authorString: Winchell J, Ma J, Krieger S.

title: From hands to tools: evidence for evolutionary precursors of tool processing in macaque cortex.
abstract: In humans, hands are animate effectors and tools are visually dissimilar inanimate objects, yet the brain represents them in closely related cortical systems. Whether this coupling depends uniquely on human tool knowledge or reflects a conserved property of primate cortex is unknown. Using whole brain fMRI (0.22 cubic mm voxels) in macaques viewing images of hands, tools, and other objects, we found that inferotemporal cortex largely followed the animate/inanimate division, with only a few small hand-tool preferring sites. In contrast, parietal and prefrontal areas showed hand-tool representational similarities that were best matched by a neural-network model trained on fine-grained human hand-object interactions rather than by networks optimized for static object recognition or general action recognition. Volumetric functional ultrasound imaging (0.0023 cubic mm voxels) independently showed that tool responses were spatially aligned with human hand, but not monkey hand, responses in posterior parietal cortex. Macaque cortex thus represents tools in relation to the hand even without habitual tool use, consistent with an evolutionarily conserved action related scaffold that may be shaped by longterm visual exposure to human hand tool interactions.

title: Does Denoising Reduce Cross-Vendor Variability in Diffusion MRI? A Travelling Heads Evaluation
abstract: Between-scanner variability in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived features can be comparable to biological between-subject variability, even for the same individual scanned at different sites. MRI harmonisation is therefore an essential tool to ensure studies are generalisable across sites, reducing between-scanner variability and enabling pooling of data to achieve large sample sizes and more representative population samples. Denoising using MPPCA is widely used in preprocessing pipelines for diffusion MRI acquisitions to improve image SNR and it has been proposed as an implicit way of harmonising data. In this registered report, we hypothesised that denoising reduces cross-scanner variability and improves reliability in diffusion MRI metrics without changing cross-scanner bias, and that susceptibility-induced off-resonance reduces its efficacy. We tested these hypotheses using a travelling-heads resource of ten subjects scanned on six scanners from three vendors (GE, Philips, Siemens), with within-scanner repeats. We found that: i) Denoising reduced voxel-wise cross-scanner coefficients of variation for fractional anisotropy (FA), mean diffusivity (MD) and mean kurtosis (MK) (BF₁₀ > 100; median -3%, -9% and -32%). ROI-wise, variability decreased for MK (-12%), increased for FA (+8%), and evidence was inconclusive for MD. ii) Contrary to our hypothesis, denoising changed cross-scanner bias in every subject-scanner pair, by up to 3% of the mean; in exploratory analyses, this change was strongly related to contrast-to-noise ratio. iii) Evidence for a change in the registered measure of reliability was inconclusive, although exploratory analyses showed higher voxel-wise reliability after denoising. iv) There was no convincing evidence that off-resonance reduces denoising efficacy. Together, these results suggest that MPPCA denoising reduces the random, noise-driven component of cross-scanner variability, most strongly at the voxel level and for kurtosis, but does not consistently reduce systematic differences between scanners. As such, it should complement harmonisation, not replace it.

title: Scalable frameworks for local evaluation of AI-enabled imaging devices using PACS-integrated large language models
abstract: Introduction: Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled imaging device performance may vary across institutions due to differences in disease prevalence, patient demographics, and acquisition protocols. Routine local evaluation, including pre-deployment baseline testing and post-deployment monitoring, remains limited by manual data curation. A large language model (LLM)-as-a-judge approach using existing radiology reports provides a method of performing local evaluation. Methods: We established PACS-integrated LLMs in HIPAA-compliant environments. We then developed two scalable frameworks to automate key processes of local evaluation: selection of a candidate series for device inference and generation of report-derived labels. We applied these frameworks to 4,000 consecutive non-contrast head CT examinations from two hospitals to evaluate agreement between radiology reports and Purple AI Hyper Insight-ICH, a commercial intracranial hemorrhage detection device. Results: For series selection, we used a three-tiered, traffic-light approach across 31,422 available series to select a single series for device inference in 3,976 examinations. For radiology report field extraction, we refined an LLM prompt with three steps: initial binary classification, characterization of discordance between the binary classification prompt output and device output, and a comprehensive prompt (featuring 28 structured fields that were informed by the preceding stages). The positive percent agreement (PPA) depended on the definition of positive cases based on the comprehensive prompt fields: it was 87.7% (79.2 to 95.0%) using similar criteria to many published studies (acute or acute-on-chronic, non-minimal, non-equivocal hemorrhage), yet was lower when including chronic, minimal or equivocal ICH. The negative percent agreement (NPA) was 94.7% (94.0 to 95.4%). Subgroup analyses demonstrated that discrepancies involving a positive device output commonly occurred in the setting of recent intracranial surgery and intracranial hyperdense (non-hemorrhagic) lesions. Conclusion: A PACS-integrated LLM approach, together with scalable frameworks for series selection and label generation, can provide radiologists with local insights about AI-enabled device performance. These insights may help radiologists interpret device outputs in clinical practice, particularly in scenarios associated with greater device-report discordance.

title: Cascading Feature Refinement with Channel-Wise Attention for Super-Resolution of Gastrointestinal Capsule Endoscopy
abstract: Wireless capsule endoscopy (WCE) now enables endoscopic examination of the whole small bowel, albeit typically in a non-invasive, more comfortable, and generally painless manner. The physical limitations of such endoscopy technology (specifically, sensor array size, battery, and light constraints) usually dictate relatively low-resolution (LR) output video frames. Consequently, capturing, and thus detecting, fine or non-protruding gastrointestinal (GI) abnormalities (e.g., small mucosal vascular lesions, mild angioectasias, and early mucosal neoplastic conditions) can sometimes be clinically sub-optimal. This paper presents a novel cascading feature refinement network involving Dense Shortcut Connections and Channel-wise Attention Mechanism (CFR-CA). The network operates on only the Luminance (Y) component of YCbCr colour space of the WCE images, exploiting high-frequency structures that are key to the GI diagnosis, while efficiently skipping processing steps on Chrominance (Cb, Cr) channels. We collected a dataset of 10,000 WCE frames from different institutions, pre-processing them by manually removing the frame corners to create our training dataset. We utilised bicubic down-sampling (x4) to generate our LR and high-resolution (HR) pairs. Experimental results show that CFR-CA achieves the best RGB Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), the best Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) on both the Y and RGB channels, and the best Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) among contemporary techniques such as SRGAN, DenseNet and RCAN, although its Y channel PSNR remains slightly below those of DenseNet and RCAN. This is expected to aid the efficacy of future CADx models, ultimately helping clinicians to accurately identify GI pathologies in WCE in a more confident and timely manner.

title: Conditional normative modeling of whole-body FDG PET/CT: inter-organ relationships outperform reference-region normalization for label-free detection of lesion-bearing organs
abstract: Purpose. Reading whole-body 2-deoxy-2-[18F]fluoro-D-glucose (FDG) positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) means judging each organ's uptake against what is expected for that patient. Clinical criteria do this with a single reference region, the liver or the blood pool. We tested whether a normative model conditioned on all other organs detects lesion-bearing organs better than reference-region normalization, without lesion labels. Methods. We analyzed the public autoPET FDG PET/CT dataset (1,014 studies; 896 patients with age and sex, 412 without malignant lesions). Models trained on control patients predicted the log maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax) of each of 34 organs, segmented with TotalSegmentator on CT, from age, sex, and the median uptake of the other organs on eroded masks, without lesion labels, which served only as the reference standard. Out-of-fold deviation scores were compared with SUVmax, liver- and blood-pool-referenced, and age-sex normative scores for detecting organs with [≥] 2 ml of lesion (1,700 organs, 355 patients). Secondary analyses included false positives per patient, repeat scans, and residual soft-tissue regions. Results. Other organs explained a median 67% of the between-patient variance in uptake, against 34% for global uptake with age and sex. The conditional linear model outperformed liver referencing: the within-patient area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was 0.916 vs 0.902 (difference 0.014, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.007-0.021), the false-positive rate at 90% sensitivity fell from 0.33 to 0.27, and at 80% sensitivity 2.9 instead of 4.3 lesion-free organs per patient were flagged. A global-uptake reference gained little (AUC 0.907). The advantage was robust to analysis choices, including a peak SUV target, and to lesion-cleaned inputs, and leveled off at about 200 training controls. Gradient boosting did not improve on the linear model, whereas modeling patient-specific variance made calibration uniform across patients. Conditional scores changed organ by organ between repeat scans, and the gain extended to mediastinal but not abdominal or pelvic soft tissue. Conclusion. Conditioning an organ's expected uptake on the patient's other organs generalizes reference-region normalization and reduces false positives in label-free detection of abnormal organ uptake, using oncology controls rather than healthy volunteers. Organ-level conditional deviations provide a calibrated, patient-specific reference on which voxel-level localization within organs can build.

title: The Developing Human Connectome Project: Fetal Data Release
abstract: The Developing Human Connectome Project (dHCP) represents a large open science resource designed to enable detailed investigations of typical and atypical brain development across the perinatal period. It consists of 1228 multimodal magnetic resonance image examinations of the fetal and/or neonatal brain from 1173 participants, together with collateral demographic, clinical, family, neurocognitive and genomic data. All subjects were studied in utero and/or soon after birth with a single MRI scanner using specially developed scanning sequences with novel motion-tolerant imaging methods and optimised for the changing properties of the developing brain. The neonatal data has been described and released separately. The fetal data release consists of multimodal data from 273 subjects scanned between 20 + 6 and 38+2 weeks (+days) of gestation, with some fetuses imaged more than once to provide longitudinal data creating 297 datasets in total. The data include: high resolution and motion corrected T1 and T2 weighted anatomical images; high temporal resolution functional and multi-shell high angular resolution diffusion MRI; and multimodal age-resolved atlases; together with demographic, family and clinical data, genomic and epigenomic data and follow-up neurodevelopmental assessment at around 18 months. This paper describes the dHCP fetal image acquisition, reconstruction and processing protocols, summarizes the available data, and provides information on how it can be accessed.

title: [MRI of suspected bone and soft tissue sarcomas - an overview].
abstract: Sarcomas are rare malignant tumors of connective and supportive tissues, associated with relatively poor five-year survival. According to Swedish patient care bundles ("standardiserat vårdförlopp"), MRI should be performed at local radiology departments before a possible referral to a sarcoma center when there is a strong suspicion of a soft tissue sarcoma, highlighting the need for adequate knowledge of appopriate MRI protocols. For soft tissue lesions, MRI is diagnostic only for a few entities, such as simple lipomas. Most muskuloskeletal tumors, however, require biopsy for definitive diagnosis. Consequently, MRI is primarily used to assess tumor extent prior to biopsy and potential surgery. The Swedish Society of Musculoskeletal Radiology (SFMSR) recommends that an MRI protocol for musculoskeletal tumors should always consist of at least the following three sequences: coronal STIR FSE, axial T1-weighted FSE, and axial T2-weighted FSE. Coronal STIR is mainly used for tumor detection and evaluation of lipomatous lesions. Axial T1 is primarily used to assess intraosseous tumor extent and characterize lipomatous lesions. Axial T2 is primarily used to evaluate soft tissue tumor extension and extraosseous components of bone tumors.

title: Presacral Myelolipoma Mimicking Liposarcoma Complicated by Massive Intraoperative Hemorrhage: A Case Report.
abstract: Introduction Myelolipoma is a benign tumor composed of mature adipose tissue and hematopoietic elements. Extra-adrenal lesions can occur in the presacral region and may mimic liposarcoma. Resection of a large presacral tumor can also cause life-threatening hemorrhage. We report a presacral myelolipoma that was difficult to diagnose preoperatively and was complicated by massive intraoperative hemorrhage. Case presentation A 71-year-old woman had an incidentally detected 75 × 75 × 125-mm presacral mass with mixed fatty and solid components on contrast-enhanced CT. MRI showed restricted diffusion, and fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT showed mild uptake (maximum standardized uptake value, 3.93). No growth occurred over approximately 3 months. Because liposarcoma could not be excluded, the patient chose open resection without biopsy for diagnosis and treatment. During cranial dissection along the anterior sacrum, massive bleeding occurred from the right internal iliac venous system, and systolic blood pressure decreased to 50-60 mmHg. Manual compression was insufficient, and massive transfusion was initiated. Intraoperatively, a vein communicating with the right internal iliac vein was found to enter the tumor, and the main trunk of the right internal iliac vein was ligated near its junction with the right common iliac vein. Persistent bleeding required ligation of a tumor-entering branch of the right internal iliac artery; the arterial main trunk was preserved. Hemostasis was prioritized, and the tumor was removed in 2 pieces; the capsule was disrupted without macroscopic tumor spillage. Diffuse presacral venous plexus bleeding was controlled with electrocautery and oxidized cellulose. Operative time was 3 h 21 min, and blood loss was 4850 mL; 10 units of leukocyte-reduced red blood cells and 6 units of fresh frozen plasma were transfused. Histopathological examination established the diagnosis of myelolipoma. No vascular complications occurred, and contrast-enhanced CT at approximately 1 year showed no residual or recurrent tumor. Conclusions Presacral myelolipoma should be considered in the differential diagnosis of fat-containing presacral tumors. In large tumors, the relationship with the internal iliac vessels and presacral venous plexus should be carefully assessed, and adequate blood products, early vascular control, and source-specific hemostatic techniques should be prepared before resection.

title: Emergency Resection for Perforated Small Bowel Metastasis from Primary Lung Cancer During Systemic Therapy: A Case Report.
abstract: Introduction Small bowel metastases from lung cancer may remain clinically occult until serious complications, including obstruction, bleeding, and perforation, occur. We report a case of perforated jejunal metastasis with a synchronous ileal metastasis at high risk of obstruction, identified during emergency surgery while several previously documented extraintestinal lesions had decreased in size. Case presentation A 75-year-old woman with metastatic non-small cell lung carcinoma favoring adenocarcinoma had a programmed death-ligand 1 tumor proportion score of 95% and no targetable alteration on the companion-diagnostic panel. Pembrolizumab monotherapy (200 mg intravenously every 3 weeks) was administered for 4 cycles; no antiangiogenic agent had been administered concurrently or previously. Eleven days after the 4th dose, she developed acute abdominal pain. CT showed focal small bowel wall thickening, adjacent extraluminal air, diffuse bowel edema, and ascites. Emergency surgery revealed a perforated jejunal tumor approximately 20 cm distal to the ligament of Treitz. Systematic examination of the entire small bowel identified a 2nd, nearly circumferential ileal tumor approximately 15 cm proximal to the terminal ileum with marked luminal narrowing; both lesions were resected. Histopathological examination showed metastatic poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of pulmonary origin. Neither tumor necrosis nor a histological treatment effect was identified, and the non-neoplastic mucosa showed no findings suggestive of immune checkpoint inhibitor-related enteritis. The patient was discharged on POD 19. Pembrolizumab was not resumed. PET-CT on POD 30 demonstrated widespread disease progression, and the patient transitioned to best supportive care. She died on POD 61 without recurrent gastrointestinal perforation, obstruction, or bleeding. Conclusions Clinically occult small bowel metastases may present with perforation or impending obstruction during systemic therapy even while previously documented lesions at other sites decrease in size. Because the intestinal lesions were not identifiable before treatment, true discordant progression could not be established. Histopathological findings supported direct tumor-related perforation rather than treatment-induced tumor necrosis or immune-mediated enteritis. Emergency source control and systematic examination of the entire small bowel may identify additional lesions that alter operative management.

title: Posterior Mediastinal Schwannoma Extending into the Retroperitoneum Resected through a Thoracoabdominal Approach.
abstract: Introduction Posterior mediastinal schwannomas are generally resected through a thoracic approach. However, giant tumors extending beyond the diaphragm into the retroperitoneum present unique technical challenges because of their proximity to major vascular structures and the potential risk of neurological complications. We report a case of a giant posterior mediastinal schwannoma successfully resected through a thoracoabdominal approach. Case presentation A woman in her 70s was found to have a 10-cm posterior mediastinal mass during a routine health examination. She initially chose observation, but the tumor gradually enlarged to 13 cm over 6 years. Fluorodeoxyglucose-PET demonstrated increased uptake (maximum standardized uptake value, 9.2 at 60 min and 10.4 at 120 min). CT showed extension from the T9 to the L2 level, with displacement of the right kidney and compression of the inferior vena cava (IVC). Because malignancy could not be completely excluded and further growth was considered likely to increase the technical difficulty of resection, surgery was performed. A right thoracotomy was initially performed, but adequate exposure of the caudal tumor was not obtained. The incision was therefore extended to the abdomen, followed by midline laparotomy and diaphragmatic incision. The liver and right kidney were mobilized, and the IVC and right renal artery were secured before deep dissection. Feeding arteries from the right T10-T12 segmental/lumbar branches were divided close to the tumor capsule, and the tumor was completely removed en bloc. The operative time was 4 h 33 min, with 691 mL blood loss. Intraoperative milk administration confirmed the absence of chyle leakage. The postoperative course was uneventful, without neurological deficit or chylothorax, and the patient was discharged on POD 10. Histopathological examination confirmed a benign schwannoma, and the patient remained recurrence-free at the 9-month follow-up. Conclusions A thoracoabdominal approach provides excellent surgical exposure for giant posterior mediastinal tumors extending beyond the diaphragm. Careful management of segmental arteries and meticulous attention to thoracic duct injury may contribute to safe resection while minimizing neurological and lymphatic complications.

title: Young-Onset Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma Developing after Allogeneic Bone Marrow Transplantation for Fanconi Anemia: A Case Report.
abstract: Introduction Fanconi anemia (FA), a rare genetic disorder, is characterized by defective DNA repair and an increased risk of early-onset squamous cell carcinoma. Although hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) improves survival, long-term survivors experience a high risk of secondary malignancies, including esophageal cancer. Owing to extreme sensitivity to chemotherapy and radiotherapy, treatment of FA-associated esophageal cancer is particularly challenging. Case presentation A 22-year-old woman with FA who had undergone unrelated allogeneic bone marrow transplantation in childhood developed esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. Preoperative endoscopy, CT, and PET showed no lymph node or distant metastases, and the tumor was staged as cT2N0M0, cStage II. Because of the anticipated severe toxicity of DNA-damaging chemotherapy and radiotherapy in FA, an upfront surgery strategy was selected. Thoracoscopic subtotal esophagectomy with 2-field lymph-node dissection achieved R0 resection. Despite the absence of radiologically or macroscopically suspicious lymph nodes, histopathological examination revealed adventitial invasion, marked lymphovascular invasion, and metastases in 3 of 25 lymph nodes (pT3N2M0, pStage IIIB). Postoperative systemic therapy was considered, but its initiation was deferred because of incomplete postoperative recovery and concern regarding treatment toxicity. Multiple recurrences became evident 4 months after surgery, before systemic therapy could be reconsidered, and the patient died 10 months postoperatively. Conclusions This case highlights the therapeutic dilemma in FA-associated esophageal cancer between substantial toxicity from standard cytotoxic therapy and the risk of undertreatment with upfront surgery. The marked discrepancy between clinical and pathological staging illustrates the difficulty of excluding occult nodal or systemic disease when neoadjuvant therapy cannot readily be administered. Previous reports suggest that reduced-dose chemotherapy or chemoradiotherapy may retain antitumor activity but can still cause substantial toxicity, indicating an extremely narrow therapeutic window. Treatment therefore requires individualized multidisciplinary decision-making, while further accumulation of detailed data on treatment intensity, toxicity, response, and outcomes is needed.

title: Storming the Castle Gates: A Case of TAFRO.
abstract: Introduction Idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease (iMCD) is a rare inflammatory syndrome, characterised by generalised lymphadenopathy and hyperinflammatory state. Histologically, it has characteristic features that are shared with secondary forms of Castleman disease. It is more common in Polynesian populations, with a prevalence of 28 per million (cf 6-8 per million). More recently, a rare subset of this disease has been identified as thrombocytopenia, anasarca, fever, reticulin fibrosis, organomegaly (TAFRO). Compared to classic MCD, these patients present more acutely with smaller lymphadenopathy, anasarca, and have thrombocytopenia as opposed to thrombocytosis. Recognition of TAFRO is important as it has been shown to have the worst prognosis of any iMCD subtype. Method We describe the case of a 54-year-old Thai female who presented with three weeks of daily fevers. Blood tests demonstrated thrombocytopenia, while positron emission tomography (PET) revealed small fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-avid lymph nodes (∼7 mm longest axis) above and below the diaphragm with splenomegaly. Bone marrow biopsy was unremarkable. Subsequent core lymph node biopsy revealed reactive features without specific features to guide diagnosis. Over the next two months, she developed anasarca and continued to have severe thrombocytopenia with daily fevers. Infectious work-up was negative, and she had trialled extensive antibiotic coverage without improvement. Results Multidisciplinary consensus supported excisional lymph node biopsy, despite a technically challenging procedure. This confirmed MCD-like features, which, in conjunction with thrombocytopenia, anasarca, fever, and splenomegaly, supported the diagnosis of TAFRO. Siltuximab was commenced with prompt resolution of clinical syndrome and laboratory abnormalities. Conclusion This case highlights the importance of multidisciplinary collaboration in reaching a diagnosis of MCD/TAFRO. It emphasises the yield of excisional lymph node biopsy compared to core when this disease is suspected, particularly in ensuring early diagnosis and thus treatment.

title: Steroid-Responsive Lymphocytic Interstitial Pneumonitis Revealing T Cell-Dominant Chronic Active Epstein-Barr Virus Disease.
abstract: Introduction Chronic active Epstein-Barr virus (CAEBV) is a rare and under-recognised lymphoproliferative disorder characterised by persistent infectious mononucleosis-like symptoms, systemic organ involvement, and significant morbidity and mortality. It predominantly affects individuals of East Asian ancestry and is driven by clonal expansion of EBV-infected T or natural killer (NK) cells. Delayed recognition is common, and without definitive treatment, prognosis is poor. Case history We present a case of a 14-year-old Chinese boy with a 4-year history of recurrent respiratory illnesses, intermittent cytopaenias, variable hepatosplenomegaly, and persistent EBV viraemia (1.3-2.2 × 104 copies/mL), with a previous episode of likely EBV-associated neuroinflammation. The diagnostic sentinel presentation was with fevers, cough, respiratory distress, and hypoxia. Imaging demonstrated diffuse bilateral airspace changes, and subsequent bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was complicated by pulmonary haemorrhage; however, cytology showed marked eosinophilia. Lung biopsy demonstrated EBV-encoded small RNA (EBER)-positive lymphocytic interstitial pneumonitis, with concurrent EBV viraemia confirming active EBV-associated disease. Treatment with intravenous corticosteroids resulted in rapid clinical, radiological, and biochemical improvement. Review of prior investigations identified detectable EBV viraemia dating back to 2023. Despite discharge on oral corticosteroids, positron emission tomography (PET) imaging demonstrated persistent FDG-avid nodularity and ongoing active disease within the bilateral lower lobes. Ultrasound-guided lymph node biopsy subsequently confirmed CAEBV with predominant T cell involvement and no evidence of lymphoma. Trio whole-exome sequencing with an immunological disorders gene panel identified no variants of clinical significance. Management Given his ongoing progression of pulmonary disease, treatment was subsequently intensified with further pulse intravenous steroids and cyclosporin. With worsening illness, T cell-dominant CAEBV, and the absence of an identifiable immunodeficiency amenable to targeted therapy, he was initiated on cytoreductive chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisolone (CHOP) as a bridge to definitive haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), the only recognised curative intervention for CAEBV.

title: [Recent advances in brain injury in preterm infants].
abstract: The incidence of brain injury in preterm infants is high, and periventricular-intraventricular hemorrhage and white matter injury are the most common types. The occurrence of these two types of brain injuries results from prenatal, intrapartum, and postnatal factors, and the pathogenesis is complex, involving hypoxia-ischemia, immune and inflammatory responses, and immaturity of brain development. In recent years, advanced technologies such as functional near-infrared spectroscopy, amplitude-integrated electroencephalography, cranial ultrasonography, and multimodal magnetic resonance imaging have been widely applied for early detection of brain injury in preterm infants and for the assessment of severity and prognosis, although the clinical value of different modalities varies. Preterm infants with severe brain injury have a poor prognosis, and current preventive and therapeutic options remain limited in clinical practice. Of these, glucocorticoid therapy is the most well-established, whereas erythropoietin and stem cell therapies remain exploratory. Therefore, avoidance of high-risk factors, early prediction, effective prevention and treatment, and improvement of prognosis remain pressing issues in clinical practice and research.

title: [Research progress on correlation between non-contact anterior cruciate ligament injury and bone bruise].
abstract: Objective To review the research progress on the correlation between non-contact anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury and bone bruise. Methods Relevant literature on non-contact ACL injury and bone bruise published in recent years was reviewed. The imaging characteristics and injury mechanisms of bone bruise, factors affecting bone bruise distribution, the associations between bone bruise and combined intra-articular injuries, and the impact of bone bruise on postoperative outcomes after ACL reconstruction were summarized and analyzed. Results Bone bruise is a common MRI finding in non-contact ACL injury, mainly involving the lateral femoral condyle and lateral tibial plateau. The typical "kissing" bone bruise pattern can reflect the abnormal loading condition of the knee joint at the moment of injury and provides important imaging evidence for inferring the injury mechanism of ACL rupture. The occurrence and distribution of bone bruise may be influenced by factors such as age, osseous morphology of the knee, and meniscal anatomical characteristics. The extent, location, and severity of bone bruise are associated with knee laxity, anterolateral ligament injury, meniscal tears, and articular cartilage injury to varying degrees. Among these, the association between lateral compartment bone bruise and lateral meniscal injury is relatively well established, while bone bruise of the medial tibial plateau may indicate occult posterior horn injury of the medial meniscus. Bone bruise may also be associated with early postoperative pain and recovery of knee range of motion after ACL reconstruction, and may increase the risk of cartilage degeneration and post-traumatic osteoarthritis. However, its predictive value for mid- and long-term knee function and clinical outcomes remains inconclusive. Conclusion Bone bruise can reflect, to some extent, the loading mechanism and severity of non-contact ACL injury, and provides important clues for identifying associated structural injuries and evaluating prognosis. However, the grading and assessment criteria for bone bruise remain unstandardized, and controversies remain regarding its associations with certain combined injuries and long-term clinical outcomes. Further standardized, large-scale, multi-center, and long-term follow-up studies are required to clarify the clinical value of bone bruise in the assessment and prognostic evaluation of ACL injury.

title: [Effect of endoscopy-assisted anterior cervical discectomy and fusion on single-level cervical spondylotic radiculopathy].
abstract: Objective To compare the clinical efficacy and safety of endoscopy-assisted anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (Endo-ACDF) versus conventional ACDF in the treatment of single-level cervical spondylotic radiculopathy (CSR). Methods Ninety-nine patients with single-level CSR treated between January 2023 and January 2025 were retrospectively enrolled, including 46 patients who underwent Endo-ACDF (Endo-ACDF group) and 53 patients who underwent conventional ACDF (ACDF group). Propensity score matching was performed, and 62 patients (31 in each group) were finally enrolled. Baseline characteristics, including age, gender, body mass index, disease duration, affected segment, and preoperative visual analogue scale (VAS) score, Japanese Orthopaedic Association (JOA) score, neck disability index (NDI), C 2-7 Cobb angle and height of the affected intervertebral space, were comparable between the two groups after matching ( P >0.05). The outcome indicators were compared between groups, including perioperative parameters (operation time, incision length, intraoperative blood loss, and hospital stay); VAS score, JOA score, and NDI before operation and at 3 days, 3 months, 6 months and 12 months after operation; radiographic parameters (C 2-7 Cobb angle, height of the affected intervertebral space, and interbody fusion); occurrence of complications. Results All operations were completed successfully. Compared with the ACDF group, the Endo-ACDF group had a shorter incision length, less intraoperative blood loss, and a shorter hospital stay, but a longer operation time, all showing significant differences ( P <0.05). All patients were followed up 12 months. In both groups, VAS score, JOA score, and NDI at each postoperative time point significantly improved compared with the preoperative values ( P <0.05). The Endo-ACDF group showed better VAS scores at 3 days, 3 months, and 6 months and better NDI scores at 3 days and 3 months than the ACDF group ( P <0.05). At 12 months after operation, the C 2-7 Cobb angle and the height of the affected intervertebral space significantly improved compared with the preoperative values in the two groups ( P <0.05), while the changes from baseline in these two parameters did not differ significantly between the two groups ( P >0.05). Bone fusion was achieved in all patients of both groups, with a fusion rate of 100%. The incidences of complications were 3.23% (1/31) in the Endo-ACDF group and 9.68% (3/31) in the ACDF group, with no significant difference ( P> 0.05). Conclusion Endo-ACDF achieved comparable efficacy to conventional ACDF in the treatment of single-level CSR, with the advantages of a clearer operative field, less surgical trauma, and faster early postoperative symptom relief and functional recovery.

title: [Early effectiveness of patient-specific three-dimensional-printed porous tantalum blocks for hip revision in patients with Paprosky type Ⅲ massive acetabular bone defects].
abstract: Objective To evaluate the early clinical and radiographic outcomes of patient-specific three-dimensional-printed porous tantalum blocks for the reconstruction of Paprosky type Ⅲ massive acetabular bone defects in hip revision. Methods The clinical data of 17 patients (17 hips) with Paprosky type Ⅲ massive acetabular bone defects undergoing revision after hip arthroplasty between January 2022 and January 2025 were retrospectively analyzed. The cohort comprised 6 males and 11 females, with a mean age of 59.4 years (range, 37-80 years). Nine patients had Paprosky type ⅢA defects and 8 had type ⅢB defects, including 5 with pelvic discontinuity. All patients underwent acetabular side (9 cases) or both acetabular and femoral components (8 cases) reconstruction with patient-specific three-dimensional-printed porous tantalum blocks combined with revision acetabular cups. Harris hip score (HHS) and visual analogue scale (VAS) score were compared between preoperative and last follow-up. The position of radiographic hip center of rotation (rCOR), acetabular cup inclination and anteversion, osseointegration, and implant stability were evaluated by anteroposterior pelvic X-ray films and CT, and perioperative complications and re-revision were recorded. Results The operation was successfully completed in all patients, with a mean operation time of 141.2 minutes (range, 80-280 minutes) and a mean intraoperative blood loss of 752.9 mL (range, 300-1 500 mL). All patients completed follow-up, with a mean duration of 22.1 months (range, 13-41 months). At last follow-up, the HHS score significantly increased from 37.0±5.8 to 87.9±3.0, while the VAS score significantly decreased from 6.0 (5.5, 7.0) to 0.0 (0.0, 1.0) ( P <0.05). The horizontal rCOR distance on the operated side improved significantly when compared with the preoperative value ( P <0.05) and did not differ significantly from that on the contralateral side ( P >0.05). The vertical rCOR distance decreased significantly ( P <0.05) but remained greater than that on the contralateral side ( P <0.05). At last follow-up, all acetabular reconstructions remained radiographically stable, with an acetabular cup inclination of (41.87±4.38)° and an acetabular cup anteversion of (19.47±3.77)°. No intraoperative screw penetration through the inner pelvic cortex or neurovascular injury was recorded. No heterotopic ossification, clinically significant limb-length discrepancy, implant mismatch requiring additional adjustment or component replacement, tantalum blocks migration, screw loosening or breakage, or aseptic loosening was observed. Postoperative venous thrombosis occurred in 2 patients, both of whom improved following treatment. No other major complication was reported. Conclusion Patient-specific three-dimensional-printed porous tantalum blocks demonstrated favorable early clinical and radiographic outcomes in the reconstruction of Paprosky type Ⅲ massive acetabular bone defects, with improvements in hip function, pain relief, radiographic stability, and restoration of the hip center of rotation. Larger multicenter and random clinical trials with longer follow-up are warranted to establish long-term outcomes and potential advantages over alternative reconstruction techniques.

To evaluate the early clinical and radiographic outcomes of patient-specific three-dimensional-printed porous tantalum blocks for the reconstruction of Paprosky type Ⅲ massive acetabular bone defects in hip revision.

The clinical data of 17 patients (17 hips) with Paprosky type Ⅲ massive acetabular bone defects undergoing revision after hip arthroplasty between January 2022 and January 2025 were retrospectively analyzed. The cohort comprised 6 males and 11 females, with a mean age of 59.4 years (range, 37-80 years). Nine patients had Paprosky type ⅢA defects and 8 had type ⅢB defects, including 5 with pelvic discontinuity. All patients underwent acetabular side (9 cases) or both acetabular and femoral components (8 cases) reconstruction with patient-specific three-dimensional-printed porous tantalum blocks combined with revision acetabular cups. Harris hip score (HHS) and visual analogue scale (VAS) score were compared between preoperative and last follow-up. The position of radiographic hip center of rotation (rCOR), acetabular cup inclination and anteversion, osseointegration, and implant stability were evaluated by anteroposterior pelvic X-ray films and CT, and perioperative complications and re-revision were recorded.

Results

The operation was successfully completed in all patients, with a mean operation time of 141.2 minutes (range, 80-280 minutes) and a mean intraoperative blood loss of 752.9 mL (range, 300-1 500 mL). All patients completed follow-up, with a mean duration of 22.1 months (range, 13-41 months). At last follow-up, the HHS score significantly increased from 37.0±5.8 to 87.9±3.0, while the VAS score significantly decreased from 6.0 (5.5, 7.0) to 0.0 (0.0, 1.0) (P<0.05). The horizontal rCOR distance on the operated side improved significantly when compared with the preoperative value (P<0.05) and did not differ significantly from that on the contralateral side (P>0.05). The vertical rCOR distance decreased significantly (P<0.05) but remained greater than that on the contralateral side (P<0.05). At last follow-up, all acetabular reconstructions remained radiographically stable, with an acetabular cup inclination of (41.87±4.38)° and an acetabular cup anteversion of (19.47±3.77)°. No intraoperative screw penetration through the inner pelvic cortex or neurovascular injury was recorded. No heterotopic ossification, clinically significant limb-length discrepancy, implant mismatch requiring additional adjustment or component replacement, tantalum blocks migration, screw loosening or breakage, or aseptic loosening was observed. Postoperative venous thrombosis occurred in 2 patients, both of whom improved following treatment. No other major complication was reported.

Conclusion

Patient-specific three-dimensional-printed porous tantalum blocks demonstrated favorable early clinical and radiographic outcomes in the reconstruction of Paprosky type Ⅲ massive acetabular bone defects, with improvements in hip function, pain relief, radiographic stability, and restoration of the hip center of rotation. Larger multicenter and random clinical trials with longer follow-up are warranted to establish long-term outcomes and potential advantages over alternative reconstruction techniques.

title: [Clinical application of patient-specific three-dimensional-printed porous tantalum biological proximal interphalangeal joint prostheses].
abstract: Objective To investigate the effectiveness and safety of patient-specific three-dimensional (3D)-printed porous tantalum biological proximal interphalangeal joint (PIP) prostheses for the treatment of PIP osteoarthritis. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted on 17 patients with PIP osteoarthritis who underwent arthroplasty using patient-specific 3D-printed porous tantalum biological PIP prostheses between January 2023 and January 2025. The study population comprised 11 men and 6 women, with a mean age of 38 years (range, 22-67 years). The affected fingers included the middle finger in 9 patients, index finger in 4, ring finger in 2, and little finger in 2. Preoperatively, the active PIP flexion range of motion (ROM) was (29.73±11.58)°, and the extension ROM was (14.62±7.10)°. The preoperative visual analogue scale (VAS) score for pain was 5.6±1.1, and the Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand (DASH) score was 37.0±4.5. The operation time, intraoperative blood loss, and perioperative complications were recorded. Active PIP flexion and extension ROM, VAS scores, and DASH score were compared between preoperation and last follow-up. X-ray film evaluations were performed to assess coronal plane alignment, periprosthetic radiolucent lines, and evidence of prosthetic deformation or fracture. Results All 17 procedures were successfully completed. The mean operation time was 67 minutes (range, 57-81 minutes), and the mean intraoperative blood loss was 50 mL (range, 30-65 mL). No perioperative complication, including skin necrosis or infection, was observed. All patients completed follow-up, with a mean follow-up duration of 8 months (range, 6-21 months). At last follow-up, the active PIP flexion ROM increased to (84.35±7.97)°, the VAS score decreased to 0.8±0.9, and the DASH score improved to 11.0±5.5, all showing significant didifferences when compared with preoperative values ( P< 0.05); the extension ROM was (21.48±12.26)°, showing no significant didifference ( P >0.05). Radiographic assessment at last follow-up demonstrated satisfactory coronal plane alignment in all patients. No periprosthetic radiolucent lines, prosthetic deformation, fracture, or subsidence was identified. Conclusion Patient-specific 3D-printed porous tantalum biological PIP arthroplasty appears to be a promising surgical option for the treatment of PIP osteoarthritis. This technique may effectively relieve pain, improve joint flexion ROM and hand function, and provide satisfactory short-term radiographic stability.

title: Decreased Synovial Fluid SLC7A11 and GPX4 Levels Correlate with Knee Osteoarthritis Disease Severity.
abstract: Background Ferroptosis has been suggested to play a role in the pathogenesis of primary knee osteoarthritis (OA). The current study aimed to explore the potential relationship between the concentrations of SLC7A11 and GPX4 in serum and synovial fluid (SF) and the severity of knee OA. Methods A total of 120 patients with knee OA and 120 healthy controls were included in this study. Serum and SF levels of SLC7A11 and GPX4 were measured using ELISA before and after a comprehensive therapeutic intervention. Radiographic severity of OA was evaluated using the Kellgren-Lawrence (K-L) grading system. Clinical severity was assessed via Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) and Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoar-thritis Index (WOMAC) scores. Levels of interleukin-6 (IL-6) and matrix metalloproteinase-3 (MMP-3) were also analyzed. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was employed to evaluate the diagnostic utility of SLC7A11 and GPX4 levels in relation to K-L grades. Results Serum levels of SLC7A11 and GPX4 did not show significant differences between knee OA patients and healthy controls. However, patients with K-L grade 4 exhibited statistically significant lower concentrations of SLC7A11 and GPX4 in SF compared to those with K-L grades 2 and 3. Furthermore, SF levels of these proteins were significantly lower in patients with K-L grade 3 compared to those with grade 2. Negative correlations were observed between SF levels of SLC7A11 and GPX4 and K-L grades, as well as with SF levels of IL-6 and MMP-3. SF concentrations of SLC7A11 and GPX4 were also inversely correlated with VAS and WOMAC scores. ROC analysis indicated that both SLC7A11 and GPX4 demonstrated good diagnostic value for assessing radiographic progression in knee OA. Conclusions These results indicate that SLC7A11 and GPX4 may function as potential biomarkers for monitoring disease progression and therapeutic efficacy in knee osteoarthritis.
